p: A strong illustration portfolio today ticks several boxes: It looks beautiful, emphasizes quality over quantity, uses clean, work-promoting layouts, and makes it easy to get in touch. They also should load fast, feel effortless for users to navigate, and beautifully adapt across screens.

In other words, that online portfolio works hard for you. These digital business cards frame your 10-15 strongest pieces in ways that amplify your voice and brand, proving you’re a confident master of the craft.

Together, these 20 standout illustrator portfolio examples show how to balance aesthetics with usability. Each one takes a different approach — minimalist grids, immersive storytelling, bold editorial layouts — so you can see how illustrator peers shape their own online presence today. Use each as inspiration for your reimagined web presence.

Artfolio uses a simple, clean grid that places artwork at the forefront, removing distractions so the viewer’s focus stays locked on the creative works. It’s the kind of layout that works well for animation styles that are bold or high-detail, as nothing competes with the art.

Plus, its sidebar contains 2-3 spots to insert links to your key socials and a prominent but unforceful “Hire Me” form link. Artfolio is perfect for illustrators and graphic designers across disciplines who just want their portfolio to feel like a clean, updated gallery.

Visual and motion animator Laura Valls’ portfolio demonstrates a clear, professional value statement with a Pinterest-style layout. Asymmetric blocks sprinkled across the homepage each preview an individual project, but with an added twist: Hover over one, and the preview becomes animated. That CSS hover effect feels energetic, modern, and lively — perfect ways to communicate your personal brand.

Alina Papazova’s portfolio immediately stands out for its use of a bold 3D hero graphic. It’s a smart and eye-catching examples for illustrators who work with 3D renders, as well as multi-medium animators who reference for how to keep their work feeling unified.
ElsasPortfolio template showing a modern, dynamic layout.

ElsasPortfolio is description-forward, sleek and modern, with plenty of breathing room between sections. Oversized imagery and generous whitespace give each piece and text the spotlight it deserves, while the responsive design ensures examples looks polished on every screen. It’s ideal for illustrators who want a contemporary, art-director-ready vibe.

Artemis offers a template for illustrators who want their work to have a clear throughline. Think narrative-driven projects whose process you walk your audience through across each of its 5 templated pages. Fully responsive, it adapts across devices without losing the punchy, playful page flow. A great choice for when you need a portfolio displaying one strong, in-depth project, collection, or collab.
Meelo portfolio template with bold hero imagery.

Meelo grabs attention immediately with bold hero blocks and clear, easy-to-follow square content frames. It feels like an upgraded creative slide deck, great for an illustration portfolio that showcasing full brand campaigns or a high-level online CV.
Plywood portfolio template with balanced typography and modular sections.

Plywood is built for fine arts storytelling. Modular sections let you layer in text right alongside your visual examples, which is gold for highlighting murals, process sketches, concept iterations, or client before and afters. It’s a strong choice for illustrators who promote not just a final outcome, but the thought and craft behind it.
Mastak portfolio template with a crisp, editorial style.

Mastak has a e-zine aesthetic — crisp grids, clear crediting space, and a consistent type system to write out project contexts. If your practice leans into series (e.g. comic book illustrators, Youtube series animators), or if your work is featured regularly in magazines, journals, or physical zines, then this publication-oriented example offers some great inspiration.
Purply portfolio template with playful colors and clean structure.

Purply brings energy to the table with a playful color palette on a clean white backdrop, similar to an actual gallery wall. It’s made for illustrators with bold, infographic-driven personal work, the kind of art that thrives in a portfolio with a bit of personality in the framing.
LaFlora portfolio template with elegant visual rhythm and ample whitespace.

LaFlora has elegance in its design DNA. Well organized, spacious sections and an airy, e-commerce-mirroring grid is user-friendly, letting viewers scroll and explore clearly categorized works. LaFlora is for animators and artists who want to represent the quiet sophistication of their work.

Vistiq uses a grid-driven layout that scales to accommodate large bodies of work. The grid keeps everything digestible while maintaining a clear logic and flow across project pages. For prolific illustrators with dozens of series or client campaigns, this is a smart way to stay organized without overwhelming portfolio visitors.
Charmant portfolio template with a minimal aesthetic.

Charmant is minimal, refined, and quietly luxurious. Clean typography lifts the work without crowding it, bringing a design approach that creates a premium, even editorial feel to featured works. It’s a great example for fashion illustrators, art directors, and other artists to promote the elegance and upscale nature of their brands.
Foresta portfolio template with strong hero sections.

Foresta leans into story-forward work. Hero visuals and a scroll-driven narrative give the site an atmospheric quality — great for illustrators working on thematic series, picture books, children’s book projects, even social media. Use it as a web design example that guides viewers through your world instead of just showing them final illustrations.
Pepper portfolio template with clean sections and crisp typography.

Pepper has a familiar user experience-minded layout, light and modern fonts, large thumbnails, and the option to fold in a shop for selling prints or commissions to potential clients. For freelancers balancing retainer client work with ad-hoc sales, the template strikes a nice balance between portfolio and storefront.
Showu portfolio template with strong hero blocks and scannable project sections.

Showu gets straight to the point with strong hero blocks and scannable project sections. Such a web design allows clients to quickly evaluate the widest breadth of your online portfolio, especially when you’re an illustrator positioning yourself for agency or brand work. If your goal is landing commercial gigs, Showu works in your favor.
Webstack portfolio template with flexible sections for mixed media.

Webstack is all about flexibility. The clear content architecture comes complemented by the surprising pops of neon, supporting contemporary artists who mix media (for example, pairing digital illustration with product design mockups or character design visuals). If you want your illustration portfolio website to show range without looking chaotic, but still surprise and inform, Webstack is a good example.
Ledger portfolio template with an understated, professional design.

Ledger has an understated, professional design that feels clean and commercial. Its consistent spacing and typography create a polished, cohesive feel across the entire portfolio without any distractions. It’s a natural fit for commercial illustrators, in-house or freelance book cover designers, and other pros who need to communicate credibility as much as creativity.

LookFolio is all about speed. Its minimal chrome design puts your grid of work front and center, making it easy for art directors or potential clients to conduct a quick but thorough portfolio review. Editorial illustrations show off especially well in this kind of template, as does advertising work.
Illustrate portfolio template with striking hero visuals.

Illustrate was built specifically for illustrators, and it shows. A striking hero section sets the tone, while focused project pages keep the emphasis on your craft. The whole template’s user experience helps set a confident first impression for freelancers and agency-represented fine artists alike.
Pearl portfolio template with an elegant and simple layout.

Pearl is simple, adaptable, and polished — a reliable starting point for illustrators building their first portfolio website or reworking an outdated one. The clean design adapts easily to different styles, letting the art take center stage. There’s also subtle spots to integrate infographics, text blocks, links to social media, pricing, and CTAs. Pearl checks all the boxes.

An illustration portfolio is part curation, part storytelling, and part technical craft. To stand out, your site needs to reflect your full-time artistic identity while being effortless to navigate and fast to load.

At a glance: Your 10 best pieces, an About page, social media links, clear contact info, and consistent design aesthetic throughout. Anything else — pricing, checkout, storyboards, or detailed web design elements — are optional, but keep the presentation cohesive.

Select a concise collection of your best illustrations. Less is more: Chose 10 to 15 pieces max, ones that accurately represent your style, technical skill, and the type of commissions you wish to attract.
Keep rotating older projects out so your site always reflects your current level. This focused selection demonstrates confidence and a clear artistic statement.

A no-code web design platform like Framer gives you both the creative control and the performance edge. Templates, SEO elements, CMS integration, and one-click publishing keep your site fast, responsive, and easy to update.
Explore templates in the illustrative and artist categories to see what’s possible.

Illustration portfolio templates such as Artfolio, Illustrate, or Plywood give you a professional backbone you can customize. Edit fonts, color, graphics, and layout elements to reflect your personal brand so your site feels both professional and uniquely yours.

Make navigation for potential clients intuitive. Standard navigation includes having sections for your Work (with preview thumbnails and optional creative hover effects), an About page, a pricing page, and a Contact page.
You might also add a Shop integration or Artist’s Journal, but only if they add value. Use CMs fields to keep your online portfolio easy to maintain.

Your portfolio must perform flawlessly on any screen. Use a platform with responsive layouts that automatically adapt to mobile, tablet, and desktop views. Compress images and test across devices. Fast load times (think sub-2 seconds) keep potential clients from bouncing before they see your work.
It’s a best practice to use JPEG for most illustrations and PNG for layered images.
An effective portfolio contains several key pages:
The homepage should immediately showcase your best work to capture attention.
Your About page tells your story, detailing your approach, expertise, and a professional photo or logo.
The Contact page provides a clear way to reach you, such as an email address or contact form, along with links to your professional social profiles.
Including testimonials, a client list, or a glimpse into your creative process can also build credibility.
Framer was built by creatives, for creatives, who want professional illustration portfolios without the coding headache.

Every site is responsive by default, so your illustrations look sharp on phones, tablets, or desktop. The visual canvases give you the precision of a design tool with the ease of drag-and-drop publishing.

Explore illustration portfolio templates on Framer Marketplace to find a starting point that fits your style. Customize fonts, colors, and layouts until it feels like yours. Or browse the Framer Gallery to see live illustrator sites already built with the platform for even more inspiration.
Create a portfolio that shows and amplifies your art. Framer helps you build a site that looks great, works fast, and grows with your career. When you’re ready, sign up for Framer to get started.

p: With tens of thousands of SaaS products on the market, your marketing website needs to cut through the noise to stand out.  A well-crafted SaaS website goes beyond simply showcasing features; it should reflect the quality of your product experience, build trust via a seamless browsing experience, and build conversion intent through social proof.
Explore more than a dozen examples of standout SaaS websites to derive inspiration for your own web design strategy.

What truly separates the best SaaS websites from the mundane are elements that blend visual storytelling with functional design to foster both emotional and rational justifications for a subscription purchase. The best SaaS websites have in common:
A clear list of features. While it seems basic, clearly showcasing a SaaS product’s standard and unique features (without overwhelming users with promotional language) is key to demonstrating value.
High-quality screenshots or GIFs. The more quickly you can demonstrate how well your product works, the more quickly potential customers can move from having questions to signing up for a demo.
Interactive demo experiences. Beyond screenshots and GIFs, these interactive demos provide an immersive experience for potential users.

Well-organized social proof. Social proof entails spotlighting customer testimonials, professional reviews, and positive user-generated content (UGC) to build trust among potential users. Many impactful websites feature client logos above the fold to immediately demonstrate legitimacy.

Intuitive user experience. Good sites have all the information you need; great sites make navigating that information quick, easy, and intuitive. Users expect to find access to product details, pricing, resources, company information, and access to a log-in portal or set-up page in the top nav, while elements like privacy policies, terms, and contact links should be available in the footer.
Read on to explore 13 examples of best-in-class SaaS website design that can inspire your own building process.

Budgeting app Copilot Money’s homepage leans into the power of social proof, with awards and accolades from Apple’s app store at the very top of the page, followed by a block of media logos, additional awards, and user reviews just beneath the hero. Logos from the New York Times, The Verge, and Tech Crunch link to published editorial reviews, while testimonials pulled from real users on X and the Apple App Store comprise the grid.

To demonstrate the app’s functionality, the landing page highlights the product’s AI-powered capabilities through an animated visualization of spending categories laid over playful 8-bit artwork of storefronts. The storefronts bear logos of recognizable financial institutions, subtly building more credibility by showcasing the array of platforms that users can connect to their Copilot account.
The sticky navigation bar at the top keeps the “Download” CTA ever-present.

Rainbow, a secure cryptocurrency wallet for individual consumers, breaks conventional crypto website design norms with its vibrant, surreal visual aesthetic. While blockchain SaaS platforms typically opt for more corporate blues and grays, Rainbow embraces bright oranges and electric pink that immediately distinguish it from competitors. This is especially noticeable in its bright CTA buttons and rainbow-emblazoned sticky navigation bar.

The homepage features a dynamic carousel of product screenshots and GIFs that demonstrate wallet functionality without overwhelming users. An interactive keyboard element—complete with rainbows that explode from the keyboard when clicked—invites exploration, transforming passive browsing into active engagement. This playful approach to SaaS design proves that even technical products can embrace personality while maintaining credibility through clear feature demonstrations.

Assemble is a product management tool designed for teams and businesses tackling complex projects. Its website design leans on a clean aesthetic and parallax effects to clearly tell its product story and reinforce its core value proposition, which is its calendar-centric UX. Visually, the brand and website are designed to evoke a feeling of zen.

Meanwhile, interactive demos, rather than static screenshots, provide a functional preview of its interface, allowing users to get a feel for the product’s core workflows (with creative flourishes). Assemble’s designers created these interactive, visual animations to help customers quickly understand complex features.

Zazu is a South African digital banking platform that provides various services for small businesses, entrepreneurs, and freelancers. Zazu’s website design effectively balances product screenshots with social validation, understanding that B2B financial software requires both functional demonstration and trust-building. It weaves the two together in an impactful credibility-building flow.

A scrolling ticker of client logos separate the hero section from the product-oriented sections that follow. Then, a testimonial carousel with a contrasting color scheme creates a natural break in the page flow. It features client photos, company logos, and direct quotes from entrepreneurs that glide across the page as the user interacts with arrow buttons, reinforcing the platform’s credibility.

Paris-based Scribe is an automated email signature platform, which allows its users to craft beautiful, on-brand email signatures and deploy them across a team or entire organization. Their site uses several multimedia features to engage users and demonstrate the product’s value.

On the homepage, an above-the-fold GIF demonstrates its core functionality. Further down, the site offers visitors an interactive ROI calculator, which transforms static value propositions into a personalized demonstration of value. The calculator updates in real-time as users input team size, daily outreach volume, and average customer value—providing concrete business justification.
Under the resources tab, the top option offers a concise, 1-minute video to explain what the product is and how it delivers value.

Play—a collaborative design tool that enables teams to design and ship iOS mobile apps—highlights its external credibility with an above-the-fold display of its Apple Design Award. The site’s tabbed interface with embedded GIFs creates an organized container for showcasing its freeform design canvas, prototyping capabilities, Apple App Clip sharing, and Play to Xcode shipping functionality.

The website’s user experience benefits from a grid layout featuring user-generated content (tagged with #MadewithPlay), which provides authentic social proof. This community-driven website design is a strong example of trust building through accolades and customer success.

Amsterdam-based Tellet is a customer research platform that conducts user interviews through AI-powered conversations. With a distinctive pink-and-green color palette, Tellet’s website uses scroll-triggered animations that progressively reveal interface screenshots of example user interviews (and product insights from those conversations) as users navigate their way down the page.

A bold typographic hierarchy, combined with clear copy, guides users through the platform’s step-by-step functionality. The website’s information architecture breaks Tellet’s features into digestible, colorful cards featuring templates of each step.

Before being acquired by OpenAI in 2024, Multi was a multiplayer collaboration platform for macOS that aimed to enable real-time screensharing and AI-powered meeting documentation. Its website embraces a dark color scheme that appeals to developer audiences while highlighting key features through contrasting elements. A standout feature is an interactive screenshare demo with moving cursors that highlight the collaborative features of the platform.

The homepage also features practical elements, including an updated changelog that provides a detailed record of product updates, bug fixes, and new features. This feature demonstrates transparency—a crucial trust signal for technical audiences. The straightforward grid layout also makes it easy for developers to quickly scan capabilities without unnecessary design flourishes like flashy animations or overly complex graphics.

A customer lifecycle management platform that helps B2C brands automate their campaigns, Bird’s website design centers around a high-quality looping video that serves as the focal point of the entire homepage. This full-width video demonstrates the product in action, providing a dynamic preview of complex CRM capabilities (like creating custom workflows and communication drip campaigns) that static screenshots can’t muster.

The vertical module structure below the hero creates a scannable layout where each feature receives dedicated space with supporting descriptions and interface previews. A module with tabs allows users to toggle between use cases, gliding between GIFs demonstrating customer flows specific to ecommerce and retail (an ecommerce cart), fintech and finance (a fintech verification flow), or SaaS (an automated lifecycle campaign triggered by a travel booking), depending on the users’ needs—as the users’ clients would see the tool’s flows in action.

As an AI-supported customer support platform, Plain’s website uses contrasting full-width modules to create a visual rhythm while highlighting its suite of features—including issue tracking, a native Slack integration, and automated workflows—with visually distinct modules. One module, for example, displays a scrolling loop of its queue features surrounded by ample white space. This deceptively simple layout evokes the sense of calm that Plain strives to provide with its all-in-one support interface.

While it appears to be a standard hero, the green, above-the-fold banner has a unique feature: a small toggle button that allows the user to toggle between a technical and non-technical POV. When clicked, the “I’m technical” button instantly adjusts the headline and subsequent copy, providing a unique opportunity for Plain to appeal to both technical and non-technical users—while making each feel considered by the designer.

Vibrant is a Danish online payment platform that combines in-store and online payment processing into one system. Its website creates visual interest using scroll-triggered animations—that fill white space with an on-trend buttery yellow—creating a natural section divider. A basic testimonial grid offers social proof through diverse customer voices, while polished product screenshots and GIFs show the software in real-life usage scenarios.

Musicfy’s AI music-generation platform employs stacking, full-width modules that create clear separation between features and maintain visual flow. The generous white space (in name only—the color palette is dark) makes complex AI capabilities feel approachable and easy to understand. The website design successfully balances the creativity that’s appropriate for a music tool with the clarity that’s essential for SaaS conversion.

An AI-powered, cloud-based video editing platform, Ozone’s website uses a black background with striking purple and blue accents to highlight its creative interface. The website features a frame that mimics their software interface and demonstrates collaboration capabilities like real-time chat, depicts some of its editing sliders, and highlights its draggable timeline view. The card-based layout efficiently organizes features through a combination of GIFs, screenshots, and descriptions. An oversized “Try for Free” CTA and sticky navigation bar create strong conversion points.

Once set up, use the integrated CMS to quickly deploy new pages, like blog posts, landing pages, and case studies—no engineering support needed.

/blog/best-fonts-for-websites/.description: Explore 25 of the best fonts for websites, from clean sans serifs to display serifs, with practical guidance on choosing, pairing, and loading web fonts.
h3: How to choose a font for your website
Font licensing, file formats, and loading performance
Web fonts vs. web safe fonts

p: Typography shapes first impressions and can instantly change how a website feels. On the web, a good font must balance style, usability, and readability. This guide shares Framer’s best practices and 25 top web fonts for your next project.

The best fonts for websites are legible at body sizes, load fast, and cover the weights and glyphs your design needs. Sans serifs like Inter, Satoshi, and Manrope suit interfaces and marketing sites, while serifs like Domine and EB Garamond fit long-form reading. Below are 25 options, plus guidance on choosing and pairing them.

Just as a voice actor’s intonation can influence whether or not a listener enjoys a podcast or audiobook, typefaces affect how people feel about what they read. According to a 2021 study,  typography choices can increase readers’ positive feelings by up to 13%.

As typefaces have evolved to suit the web, designers have many usability factors to consider beyond the way fonts can make people feel. When choosing web fonts, qualities like weight variability, how many languages a font comes in, and load time and availability across devices all matter.
To choose the best fonts for your website designs, find Framer’s best practices, as well as a roundup of the best web fonts, below.

Fonts like Open Sans and Lato are everywhere for a reason: They’re easy to read, comprehensive, and versatile. But you don’t have to stick to the most ubiquitous fonts to find the best fit for your current project. Here’s what to look for when choosing web fonts:
It takes about 50 milliseconds for users to decide whether to stay on your site. If your site’s typography is difficult to read, visitors may not stick around.

Legibility is all about balance: A legible font will have lower-case letters that are tall enough to make out easily, but not so tall as to be confused with upper-case letters. Its strokes will vary in width but not so much that the eye can notice it.

Last, some fine details such as serifs can help the eye draw connections from one letter to the next, but too much connection and decoration can distract. Factors like space between letters can also play a role—once again, you’re looking to strike a balance.

Downloading a luscious typeface only to discover it lacks the breadth of weights, glyphs, and languages needed for your project is a fast-track to frustration (and wasted time). When you’re browsing fonts, make sure the font family includes multiple weights. Ideally it is also variable, meaning the weight can change dynamically from its thinnest to thickest weight within the same font file. The more thorough your selection, the more flexible your site design will be over time.

For any font you use, read the licensing rules carefully to ensure you or your client has the rights to use the typeface as you intend. While common, neutral fonts on services like Google Fonts are open source, meaning they are free to use commercially, many bespoke or unique typefaces are only available through a paid license or foundry subscription.
Whether securing licensed files from a font foundry or downloading open source fonts, make sure you get a WOFF/WOFF2 file, not a desktop-only file like OTF or TTF.

File format also affects speed. WOFF2 files are the smallest, and every family and weight you add is an extra download, so load only what the design uses. Page speed affects both rankings and conversions, so treat fonts as part of your performance budget.
When building with Framer, you can use open source fonts from Framer’s own collection You can also upload your own custom fonts (though beware of how custom fonts can slow load times).

Inter is a functional, clean sans serif typeface designed for easy readability. It was created in San Francisco by Rasmus Andersson, a Swedish engineer, in 2017. It’s been updated to be used by anyone, anywhere: it has over 2000 glyphs, 147 languages, and variable weights, making it a good choice for pretty much anything.

Designed by Deni Anggara for the Indian Type Foundry, Satoshi is a geometric sans serif with an industrial feel. The tension between geometric playfulness and sans serif utilitarianism makes it an inviting font style. Satoshi could bring an approachable, design-centric brand to life in a variety of industries, whether it’s a design firm or a consumer packaged goods brand. While it has a relatively small glyph library, it’s variable and supports 10 weights and 135 languages.
Design-forward brands, consumer packaged goods, ecommerce, portfolios

Manrope is a modern sans serif font designed with versatility in mind, making it suitable for both digital and print environments. With its balance of geometric structure and humanist details, Manrope feels approachable while retaining a sense of refinement. Its wide weight range supports everything from subtle body copy to bold headlines, ensuring readability and visual impact at any scale. Compared to more rigid sans serifs, Manrope’s smoother curves and open forms convey clarity and warmth, making it well-suited for contemporary, user-friendly design.
Tech, startups, and modern consumer brands

While traditional typefaces have thin horizontal strokes and thick vertical strokes, a reverse-stress typeface like Ribes has the opposite. The resulting look is a funky, unfamiliar look that stops you in your tracks. With its nostalgic feel and eye-catching geometry, this playful typeface is a good fit for brands with an offbeat and slightly retro identity. Ribes comes to Framer through the Collletttivo foundry, and was designed by Luigi Gorlero to include three weights.
Modern designs with a retro twist
Food and beverage, entertainment, design-forward brands

With its balanced shape and smooth curves, Aspekta is a typeface you can count on to support legibility and versatility. Like Inter, Pretendard, and Helvetica, Aspekta is neutral enough that with the right styling, it can feel intellectual and innovative or swaggy and on-trend. Variable and available in 20 static weights and 18 languages, Aspekta is a fit for a wide variety of branding, ecommerce, and marketing use cases.
Outdoor gear, home goods, or fitness brands

Designed specifically for long reads on the web, Domine brings the tradition of print newspapers and magazines into the internet era. By shortening the serifs, designer Pablo Impallari of Impallari Type made Domine easy to render on-screen even at tiny sizes. The nostalgic reader longing for the days of poring over a magazine feature at the breakfast table will feel at ease with Domine.
News media and blogs, stationery brands, publishing companies

Another reverse-stress typeface, Ojuju’s designers Chisaokwu Joboson and Mirko Velimirović took inspiration from traditional African dance costumes as well as 1970s African movie posters. Available in variable and seven fixed weights, Ojuju is as versatile as it is show-stopping.
Entertainment, food and beverage, home goods

Designed for the eponymous branding agency Instrument, this typeface updates vintage serif typefaces for the internet age. Since its condensed style makes it less legible at smaller sizes, it’s recommended for display type that feels just a little irreverent, just as any good branding agency should be.
News media and blogs, stationery brands, agencies

Designer Jeremy Tribby drew inspiration from California’s public infrastructure to create Barlow, a versatile san serif font that’s also available in semi condensed and condensed versions. The resulting range makes Barlow a typeface that can hold an entire brand on its own without needing a second font, from statement display moments to dense body copy. Barlow is a good fit for projects with a social good or civic engagement component.
Public-facing services, food and beverage, tech, fitness

Chakra Petch is a unique statement font out of the iconic Thai foundry Cadson Demak. Its tapered corners have a geometric effect that can make the font look either etched in glass or pixelated, giving designers a wide aesthetic range to play with. For all its playfulness, Chakra Petch is still highly legible, even in italics, making it a strong fit for a wide variety of sites.

With Chevron detailing and side-eye counters (meaning the interior of rounded letters form a sideways teardrop shape, rather than a circle), Unbounded is just unique enough to catch your eye without overwhelming it. Unbounded’s creators believe this typeface is the first funded on blockchain, making it an apt choice for tech and finance-focused brands.

A condensed sans serif with rounded corners, Tanker feels like it belongs on a movie poster for a war documentary or a sign at a protest. It’s making a statement, but its rounded details give it a soft, inviting dimension.

Developed by the U.S. General Services Administration to modernize government websites, Public Sans is intentionally neutral. It prioritizes legibility and accessibility, making it a strong choice for professional websites in the public-facing, legal, or financial arenas.

Collletttivo calls Ortica a “calligraphic serif” because of its round curves and sharp serifs. Its Angular version recalls a cut gemstone, making the reader think of tableware or stained glass windows. Used as a big, splashy display font, Ortica has a dazzling energy.
Food and beverage, hospitality, luxury brands

Based on a fixed-width font but updated to improve legibility, Space Grotesk will feel immediately familiar to software engineers and designers. Interesting at any weight and inclusive of a wide range of glyphs, Space Grotesk is a good fit for any tech-forward modern project.

Cabinet Grotesk’s pinched stroke connections and curvy terminals make it feel more playful than your average sans serif, while still being easy to read. With a huge range of glyphs and ligatures, its designers at Indian Type Foundry intended it for use in editorial design. Cabinet is the perfect choice for a brand looking to bridge its modern web presence with the long tradition of sharp editorial print design.

It’s hard to find a cursive font that doesn’t feel dated, cheesy, or completely illegible, but Pencerio fits the bill. With a large glyph library and even stroke weight, this font can hold its own on all things elegant, from invitations to editorials.
Elegant, modern designs with a hint of vintage

Designed by Indian Type Foundry to be used at extremely large sizes, Stardom is the headline typeface of a magazine designer’s dreams. It recalls the print glory days of magazines like Vogue and Elle, while its edgy descenders make it feel new.

Zodiak is what its designers call a “sturdy” serif, with strong terminals and a huge range of characters. Whether you’re setting a juicy headline or dense body copy, Zodiak conveys a sense of old world sophistication mixed with a modern versatility. This typeface is a good fit for brands positioning themselves as thought leaders or tastemakers.

Melodrama’s high-contrast stroke weights communicate high drama, whether it’s on-screen or after hours. Picture it on an old Hollywood noir movie poster or at the top of a menu at a smoky club, making it a good candidate for a lifestyle site that knows exactly who it is.
Nightlife, food and beverage, entertainment, or hospitality brands

Used in over a million websites, Archivo is a high-performance typeface with American roots in headline typography. Since 2021, it’s been available as a variable font, stretching from ultra-thin to ultra-heavy weights and increasing its versatility.

A modern revival of a foundational typeface originally created in the 16th century, EB Garamond was updated in 2019 to be variable and web-friendly. Its low-contrast strokes and soft serifs feel like they were just set in ink, even on the crispest of modern screens.

Originally designed as a fallback for the Cooper Black, Caprasimo has the vintage feeling of a 1970s textbook or album cover. It shines at large sizes that emphasize its curved terminals and heavy ligatures, which feel soulful and fun at the same time.
Apparel and accessories brands, book covers, music and entertainment projects

Like Instrument, this condensed, vintage-inspired serif designed by Théo Guillard is best for headlines: Its off-kilter stroke connectors make the greatest impact at a large size. Try Gambarino in an advertisement for a canned cocktail or a sustainable cotton brand.
Food and beverage, hospitality, home goods

With its round features and sassy, simple details, Epilogue feels like it belongs on a cocktail menu in the 1980s Italian countryside. And with 18 styles, it feels almost like a pair of fonts rather than one big family.
Classic designs with a European flair
Most websites need two fonts at most: one for headlines and one for body text. Pick pairs with clear contrast in style but similar proportions.
Pair a display or serif headline with a neutral sans serif body, such as Stardom with Inter
Keep body text in a workhorse font with at least four weights
Match x-heights so the pair feels consistent across sizes
Stop at two families and build hierarchy with weight and size instead

When people say “web fonts,” they usually mean fonts that have been defined in a site’s CSS, are being hosted online, and were uploaded to a server in a web-optimized format such as WOFF/WOFF2 files. But just because a font is on the web doesn’t mean it’s necessarily a web-safe font.
In order for a font to be web-safe, it should be able to load even when a server or custom font file fails. To do so, the font needs to be installed on the user’s device.

In the early days of the web, font styles lived in HTML and depended on fonts installed on the visitor’s computer, which is why so many early sites used Times New Roman, Arial, and Tahoma. Custom fonts arrived with CSS support around 2009, and sites could pull in far more interesting typefaces.

Today, a small selection of fonts, like Arial and Times New Roman, usually come pre-installed on all devices. These fonts are web-safe, while a more modern typeface like Barlow would simply be considered a web font.
Use a web font from this list for your brand typography
Set a web-safe fallback such as Arial or Georgia in your font stack
Check that headings and layout still hold up when the fallback renders

Framer allows you to choose the best font for your project right from the platform: in addition to a comprehensive library of open source fonts, you can also easily upload your own font to use in any site design.
Once you’ve chosen your perfect fonts, sign up for Framer and get started with one of the reusable website templates in the Framer Marketplace.

/blog/artist-website-examples/.description: Artist websites are essential for showcasing your work. Explore 20 beautiful artist website examples that highlight stunning artist website design and inspire your own creative portfolio.
h3: Fine art and painting website templates
How to create a great artist website
Simplify designing your artist website with Framer
How Planhat scaled a Framer website with a small team
12 of our favorite marketing agency websites in 2026
12 of our favorite healthcare website templates in 2026
p: It’s no secret your online presence is tied to making a living as a full-time artist. Think of it as your personal digital studio, open to the world and accepting commissions.

It’s also essential to have an online artist portfolio in a time when clients, gallery visitors, collaborators – even curious browsers – expect a peek behind the creative curtain to commission work. That holds true across artistic mediums: from painters and traditional fine artists to commercial graphic designers, mixed-media creatives, and local tattoo artists.  See Why choose Framer for portfolio website building?.

Your artist website needs to feel as unforgettable and emotive as the work you create. The right artist-specific template makes that simple, allowing your aesthetic, process, and artistic lens to speak.
These inspiring artist website designs fall into five categories: fine art/painting, illustration/animation, photography/videography, physical media, and digital media/graphic design.
Explore these templates and get inspired to create your portfolio.
Useful design elements for painters and fine artists to include on their websites include:
Generous white space and framing, to let textures, brush strokes, and color depth breathe.
Page formatting that mirrors a gallery space or museum.
High-resolution image galleries, with minimal cropping or unwanted scaling distortion.
Clean navigation that highlights your best series, exhibitions, and catalogues, past and present.
A strong color experience (color mode toggles, dark/light theme) so the presentation of your work stays true to your fingerprint.

Strida is especially good for painters whose work contains rich texture and experimental forms. The template’s central design features large, canvas-style image blocks on each of its 8 templated pages, paired with an editorial sidebar for easy navigation. It also supports fullscreen slide transitions, and load time-reducing optimization even for your high-resolution uploads.

By Essa DonzoIf you want to showcase your art in an intuitive gallery-style portfolio, Artboard is your template. It contains a core “Project” page ideal for artists’ looking to re-create a gallery visit online. Its additional touches include thoughtful typography, soft page and scroll transitions, and solid categorizing so painters can group works by color, theme, or period.

By Blush CreativeDon’t let the name fool you. Makeup doubles as an expressive structured portfolio particularly well-suited for painters, tattoo artists, and fine artists who need to organize pages by theme. It carries a softer visual mood, a unique asymmetrical layout, and overlapping page elements mimicking actual brush strokes.
On the functional side, it provides visual breakpoints for different screen sizes and supports both dark and light themes so color consistency remains intact.

By Nick StepukHaze allows artists to pick their five best pieces, then features each on its own dedicated page “slide.” That approach offers a straightforward but strategic way for artists to communicate their portfolio without overwhelming clients. L
Likewise, Haze keeps on-page text to a minimum so attention stays locked on the art. Its strict alignment and cohesive page grid stays consistent across all five pages.
Top features for illustrators and animators to keep in mind picking a website include:
Bold headlines and playful motion effects
Dedicated pages for things like character sheets, storyboards, or concept work
Templates making it easy to show the process of your work (from sketch to final)

By Joe LiuArtemis’ stands out as an animator-friendly website thanks to its simple-to-build “Work Detail” page. This allows animators and illustrators to feature several of your career-spanning best projects, then add brief but relevant descriptions behind the full creation process. Plus, Artemis’ hover reveals allow animation previews and short image loops, while its customizable layered backgrounds on every page gives more spots to subtly feature your work.

By Satto.studioGualdi is modern and minimalist, with a striking black-and-white palette. It provides an entire 7-page website template built around “illustration frames,” a gallery-style grid layout for artists to showcase up to 12 works per page. Functionally, Gualdi has a responsive layout that preserves illustration details across screens, and CMS support for multiple projects or series.

By NutsDevFor those creating animation loops or sequential illustrations, REVIX allows previews via thumbnails, animated microinteractions, and smooth scrolling between piece series. Artists will appreciate its balance of playful motion as the self-branded “Art Gallery Website.” On the backend, adjustable project sections, file format compatibility, and mobile breakpoint tuning make this template particularly friendly for animators’ work.

By Anton RadionovSynthCreator delivers when you want your illustrations to flow on a single page, in one linear, sequential presentation. Its overall design mirrors a digital scrapbook, with work scattered across strategic white space. Customizable touches like animated scroll triggers makes the on-page experience pop, while a preview overlay feature means audiences can see sketches in their before/after state.
Photographers and videographers have several unique elements to prioritize when designing their websites:
Full-width or edge-to-edge displays, to ensure media feels as immersive as possible
Functional website support for smooth video playback, embedded clips, slideshows, and key hover effects
Dark mode options to avoid washed-out images. (Much more common with white or light-toned color schemes. Most photography sites are recommended to be dark mode.)
Technical work descriptions (e.g. camera lens and settings)
Clear, high-resolution work download or print options.
Indexy puts photography front and center, without any fluff. It’s a no-frills and focused full-screen, one-page template designed for straightforward artists to showcase their core work.

Containing sharp static typography that overlays images, Indexy provides just enough detail to contextualize the chosen photography, with generous whitespace and shadows adding contrast. Indexy additionally contains responsive image sizing, so photos stay uncompromised across screen types.

By Lunatique DesignOsei’s website template works particularly well for specialty photographers and videographers (e.g. niche commercial videographers, wedding photographers, etc.) who want to feature themselves as much as their portfolio.

Its layout flows from a static grid gallery in the “Home” and “Service” pages into more customizable sections, where you can aspect-ratio lock photo and video embeds. It also carries an “About” page with extra features and details. On the backend, it includes video light-boxes, poster-frame thumbnails, and lazy loading to keep performance tight.

By Anisa OktarianiBoardaFolio stands out for its dashboard-style design. It’ll feel familiar and intuitive not just for viewers to navigate, but for artists who want a well-organized, project-focused personal portfolio. Creatives will notice its nine templated pages balance visual-heavy previews themselves, followed by pages dedicated to written-out “Thoughts.” It’s a balanced artist website for photographers, videographers, and creatives to fully narrate their work – to show and to tell.

By Arkuš DesignPlyń is for minimalist artists. Its aesthetics best reflect portfolios that are monochromatic, strong, architectural, and ultra-contemporary. Plus, it carries several sleek functional page elements, such as fade transitions and a fluid slide-based scroll. For minimalist videographers, Plyń supports video embedding with scrub previews, responsive breakpoints, and metadata overlays so your viewers can read important details behind every preview.
Useful design elements for sculpture-heavy portfolios:
Spatial photography (lighting, shadows) to capture depth
Clean backgrounds and minimal distraction so the form and material speak
Contact or commission details made prominent (pricing, scale and transport)

By PlaiterMass, initially designed for content creators’ website, adapts artfully for physical-media portfolios: think ceramics, sculpture, glassblowing, printmaking, and more. It has a simple vertical dashboard layout to organize your work by type or theme. Once clicked, each page then contains a clear modular layout and spacious built-in galleries for artists to display their art in multiple angles and spatial contexts. Designers will notice how Mass’ lightbox views also toggle between perspectives, lending a complementary contrast to every piece.

By WizeSeasons offers strong, full-screen visuals and clean sectional breaks. It’s ideal for studio owners and artists looking for a no-fluff website, one that’s easy to navigate and lets their work shine. The template provides plenty of whitespace around imagery to avoid visual clutter. On the backend, it handles high-res image uploads and responsive scaling, so photos of large media remain impressive even on mobile.

By Flowit SupplyNaoto Studio works well to feature the process behind tactile media – not just the media. Its layout offers both full-width visuals and carousel galleries, great for sequences of form, multi-angle, or scale shots. Designers will like the custom page shadow and light customizations, its user-friendly CMS, and its added text boxes to write the story behind your work.

SLANTSUAL describes itself as “the visually striking portfolio template designed for 3D artists, architectural firms, and interior designers.” That tells you a lot about its main elements. Every page centers a portfolio piece, with sections to detail that piece’s story and process. Slantsual also contains tons of custom interactions, layered overlaps, dynamic animations, and customizable page visuals around shadow, texture, and image depth. It’s a strong, comprehensive website builder for any artist serious about the creative process as well as its output.
Digital and graphic artists should consider these key website design elements:
Clarity around deliverables, process, version history, and notable past clients
Layouts that organize strong vector work
Ability to embed interactive content (e.g. SVGs, animations, web-components)
Strong typography emphasizing your creative point of view

By PentaclayOpalhaus©’ strong, geometric layout contains 13 plug-and-play pages. Artists and studios alike have everything you need inside highly customizable pre-built templates, including pages designed for commercial intent (pricing, contact forms, even privacy and changelogs). Visually, Opalhaus© carries a sharp, modular grid layout, asymmetrical breaks, and vector texture treatments. Graphic designers especially will appreciate the precision of line-weight, typographic contrast, and strategic negative space. Functionally, it supports SVG embedding, high-def visuals, and a clean CMS.

By Cristian MieluPlywood’s aesthetic is light and playful, great for both commercial digital artists as well as experimental designers. It uses tiled images, hover effects to reveal previews, and comes with several dynamic background variations. Perhaps most useful, Plywood also contains Frameship, a popular Shopify integration. That integration simplifies business functions like secure checkout and non-commissioned inventory management.

Mugen is one of the few artist website examples designed to earn creatives retainer work. Standout features include a case study-oriented design to better highlight the process and results of your art, plus thoughtful commercial and conversion-focused details. Using Mugen as your online portfolio makes for an exceptional digital business card. Especially when its retainer purposefulness gets paired with its dramatic black color scheme, modular layout, sharp page transitions, and a distinct visual hierarchy.

Pokota’s nine pre-built pages let digital and graphic artists promote their personal brand. You get a balance of interactive elements, high-resolution images, and room for text to describe your work. All come wrapped up in Pokota’s signature bold color accents. It also includes a user-friendly CMS and SEO optimization features so your work is seen by your ideal audience.
The best artist websites combine aesthetic integrity with commercial intent, along with a smooth experience. The goal is to keep visitors fully engaged with your work and inspired to explore more.
To do so, your website, at a minimum, should do the following:

Emphasize your process. Whether painting, sculpting, illustrating, or digitally designing, people are drawn to how things are made. A “behind-the-scenes” slider, time-lapse, or sketch gallery lends depth and relatability to your portfolio.

Use the highest-quality imagery possible. Blurry or compressed images undercut professionalism. Aim for crisp photos that capture material, texture, and scale, or pages using shadows, lighting, and detail.

Build an intuitive page flow. Visitors should move seamlessly from your homepage’s hero section to project galleries through your bio and contact forms. That logical hierarchy keeps exploration – and commissions – frictionless.

Choose a responsive, mobile-first design. Many collectors, curators, and fans will see your work first on their phone. Opt for a responsive website template with layouts, images, and interactions that resize accordingly.

Have 2-3 clear calls to action (CTAs). Whether “see all exhibitions,” “commission me,” or “buy this work,” meaningful prompts let interested visitors take the next step. Make them visible and cohesive with the rest of your design.

Include an email/mailing list. Your website should feel like a two-way conversation with your patrons. An email newsletter not only builds personal thought leadership, but is often how you land more work.

Results convince when the reader can trace them. For each project, cover five things:
Contribution: what you personally owned versus what the team delivered
Baseline: where the metric stood before you started
Strategy: the decision you made and why
Metric: the number that moved, and over what period
Outcome: what the change meant for the business, such as revenue, pipeline, or retention
One traceable result per project beats a wall of vanity metrics.

Marketing portfolios present your professional story with clarity, impact, and a touch of web design sparkle. It should read like a sharp narrative of your career – clear, compelling, and visually engaging. At its best, it captures the results you’ve driven while weaving in just enough design flair to stick in someone’s mind.
To hit that balance, here are the core elements every marketing portfolio needs.

Homepage: The homepage acts as your initial handshake and intro. It presents a clear value proposition, concise 1-2 lines describing the unique value your work offers, all alongside a professional photo and a declaration of who you help.

About: An about page provides a narrative of your professional journey and expertise. It details your story, your specific market positioning or niche, and credibility markers such as awards or certifications.
Work samples: This section is a curated gallery of your best projects. Select work that aligns with the types of clients, employers, or roles you value. How far you niche down is up to you.

Case studies: A case study is an in-depth analysis of a single project. It methodically outlines the problem, key metrics, your step-by-step strategic approach, its execution, and the final measurable results.

Testimonials: Testimonials are quotes from previous clients or managers that serve as social proof. They connect your marketing portfolio to actual business outcomes, nurturing buy-in, credibility, and trust.

Contact form: This section offers direct ways for potential clients or employers to connect with you. Make sure yours is responsible and mobile-optimized, as you don’t know how leads will prefer to get in touch.
What’s more, content within a digital portfolio should organized using specific best practices that enhance readability and flow. These practices ensure your message is remembered, not just read:

Visual hierarchy: This principle guides a visitor’s attention through the page. Leading with your most significant work and using clear headings for different sections allows for easy scanning and information retention.

Results-focused: Demonstrating the impact of your work involves using specific metrics. Key performance indicators (KPIs) should focus on results decision-makers universally care about: time saved, money earned, customers captured, etc.
Personal branding: A consistent application of colors, typography, and a professional voice helps define your personal brand. This consistency reinforces your unique identity.
Scannability: Structure content for quick comprehension. Employing short sections, bullet points, and visuals in place of dense paragraphs to make messaging more digestible.

It’s not just about the look. Your portfolio has to work. The technical layer makes sure your site is discoverable, fast, and usable across devices. These behind-the-scenes details are what make the experience glitch-less:
Mobile responsiveness: A responsive design automatically adjusts your site’s layout to fit any screen size. Testing across different “breakpoints” ensures a consistent experience on all devices.
Performance: Website performance relates to how quickly pages load. This is improved by optimizing image sizes, limiting heavy embedded content, and using lazy-loading for media.

SEO: SEO helps your portfolio appear in search results. This involves using relevant keywords in titles, headings, and meta descriptions, and adding schema to help search engines understand, then index, your content in top results.

Accessibility: An accessible website is one that’s usable by people with disabilities. This includes providing sufficient color contrast for text, adding alt text to describe images, and ensuring keyboard-friendly navigation.
The smartest way to showcase your marketing chops is through a polished portfolio site that feels as intentional as your campaigns.

h1: 15 classic 90s websites + modern sites keeping the aesthetic alive
h3: Recreate the 90s-inspired website of your dreams with Framer

p: There’s today’s polished minimalism, and then there’s the internet of the 1990s. Those earliest days of the world wide web used sites as a canvas for raw expression, an era defined by personality-driven chaos that continues to captivate designers and nostalgic users alike.

The look and feel of 90s website design was unmistakable. Neon color palettes, static pixelated images, table-based layouts, and custom cursors defined the aesthetic. This style was born from technical constraints like slow dial-up speeds and limited CSS.

Fast-forward to 2026, and modern web design has made huge gains in accessibility and performance. Yet some of the expressiveness has faded. There’s an opportunity to bring back that personality-forward visual style with modern quality standards.

Here are fifteen classic 90s websites that defined the early world wide web (back when it was still called that, unironically). Many of these old-school websites are preserved in Wayback Machine archives, giving you a peek into the digital past.

This promotional site is a time capsule of classic 1996 web design, featuring a tiled starfield background, low-res animated GIFs, and navigation built on clickable image maps. The content is organized within rigid table-based grids. A mirror of the original site is still live, testifying to the iconic status of late 90s to early 2000s design trends.

The early Yahoo! homepage functioned as one of the world wide web’s most popular digital directories, presenting a dense list of blue text links with minimal graphics. The layout was strictly defined by tables, organizing a massive amount of information into a compact, anchor text-heavy portal. The site is live, but in a modern form; originals are accessible via web archives.

GeoCities’ massively popular personal website pages were the embodiment of do-it-yourself 90s website design, known for user-uploaded tiled backgrounds, blinking text, and busy sidebars. Features like “guestbooks” and “under construction” icons were common. While the service is defunct, but its pages are preserved in places like the Internet Archive.

NASA’s early web presence was practical, using stark, functional layouts with standard system fonts like Times New Roman. Inline images with text captions delivered information efficiently, and navigation was purely utilitarian.
NASA maintains a strong, multi-functional web presence today. But its original look offers a window into peak 90s design pragmaticism.

Can you talk about the evolution of the internet without talking about Microsoft? The tech OG’s Windows 95 used design elements from its namesake operating system, including beveled buttons and window-like visual frames. It served as a software promotional hub, using sliced images to create a splash-style landing page. Designers can still view that archived original site to witness a key moment in software marketing.

As a major internet portal, AOL’s site used bold, colorful banners and inline promotional blocks to guide users. Its information architecture relied heavily on HTML framesets, a technique that loaded different parts of a page independently. The site is still live but has been completely redesigned.

The very first version of Amazon launched in 1995 as a text-heavy, books-only e-commerce experience. The design prioritized book information, using standard blue hyperlinks, small and often pixelated cover images, and dense metadata to create a functional online bookstore. The current site is a modern e-commerce behemoth, but early versions available in web archives are a portal into the past.

CNN’s early site organized breaking news into multi-column table layouts, mimicking a newspaper. It used marquee-style scrolling headlines and small image thumbnails to deliver a high density of information quickly. The site is still live, with its 90s versions found in web archives.

In the late 90s, Apple’s site heavily featured product hero graphics and UI elements with beveled, three-dimensional cues. It used sliced images to construct more complex visual layouts for the era, and maintained clunkier navigation and sidebars. The modern site is live and ultra-sleek, with its past designs archived for review.

Netscape’s site was built to encourage downloads of its browser, featuring prominent CTAs and some of the earliest examples of on-page, trust-building badges. It used simple gradients, saved as tiled background images, for visual depth. The original site often serves as a relic reminding all of the very first browser popularity wars.

AltaVista is often compared to Google before Google. As an early search engine, it featured a minimalist interface focused almost entirely on the search bar. Below that main function, it offered dense directories of links, a common feature for old-school websites of the 90s that doesn’t visually stand the test of time, but certainly captures the UI of the era.

Lycos was a classic 90s informational portal, packing its homepage with modules for news, weather, and finance headlines. The layout was crowded, with a footer full of anchor links, designed to be a user’s primary doorway for the wider web. The site remains and has since been redesigned, with its original form viewable in archives.

Hotmail’s website design was as 90s functional as you could get, with a utility-focused user interface. It contained simple HTML-based web forms, standard system fonts, and a framed layout guiding users through its login and email-checking process. While now part of Outlook, Hotmail’s original design still serves as a reference point even for contemporary login sequences.

Similar to GeoCities, Angelfire hosted personal pages that showcased the best vibes of 90s internet aesthetic. Animated GIF-like dividers, static memes, visitor counters, and custom-patterned wallpapers were staples of these user-created sites. The service is still live, but the classic community pages are mostly found in WayBack Machine archives.

The website for the ICQ messaging service was built around its brand and product, featuring badge-like logos and chunky iconography. The primary goal was to get users to download the software, so large download buttons were a key design feature — and became a modern web development staple.
The spirit of these old school 90s websites lives on, but today’s tools allow creators to adopt the best of its aesthetic without the technical limitations.

Modern sites can capture the expressive freedom of 90s website design while delivering the performance and usability now expected. Here are a few examples and resources selected by web design and dev experts, and available in Framer’s Marketplace and Gallery.

This retro-immersive portfolio template recreates the classic Windows 98 user interface, complete with familiar window chrome, icons, and status bars. However, it has a modern technology backbone, meaning a responsive layout that adapts to all devices, plus a CMS for easy site updates. It provides pixel-precise nostalgia without the slow performance of legacy websites.

DeskTales offers a vintage desktop experience, using quirky, draggable windows and nostalgic navigation-bar icons to emulate a 90s workstation. While the feel is retro, the site is fully responsive, features smooth navigation, and includes simple SEO and content management elements. It’s a template that channels the light, playful nature of early personal homepages.

Both GeoCities and 1996 Space Jam website walked so Cameron’s World could run. You can immediately see the reference points, with the Cameron’s World project a sprawling digital homage built entirely from archived GeoCities page fragments. It celebrates the uncurated creativity of the early web with a loud, chaotic, collage-like arrangement of animated GIFs in tiled background patterns, and wonderfully eclectic typography.

This time-capsule plugin allows designers to apply 90s-style animated effects to any element on a Framer site. Think VHS, arcade, and glitch shaders that bring a bold, pixel-era flair to modern layouts. These effects are powered by WebGL for high performance and run natively in Framer, offering tasteful 90s motion without any external dependencies.

Windows93 is nothing short of a trip down memory lane. It’s a deeply interactive homage to 90s computer interfaces, presented as a complete operating system within the browser, and powered by retro JavaScript, CSS, and HTML elements. The experience features a pixel art environment, skeuomorphic buttons, and draggable pop-up windows that perfectly mimic early desktop computing. It’s a masterclass in nostalgic interaction design.
Creating a website that captures the 90s internet aesthetic is more than achievable, thanks to Framer’s full-site templates.
With Framer, you can blend vintage visuals with modern performance standards, making sure your site is both expressive and fast.
For example, GPU-accelerated effects, available through plugins like the Framer Shader Pack Retro, can replicate the animated GIF motion of the early world wide web without its performance issues.

Framer’s 2,000 plug-and-play templates bring modern responsiveness. While websites from the 90s were built for a single, fixed-width desktop view, Framer sites are built to adapt to any device with responsive breakpoints. Your users get the charm of retro web design, without the slow load times and glitching displays.

Finally, templates have professional infrastructure built-in. Features like global hosting, integrated settings for traffic-vital SEO, and one-click publishing are standard. This ensures your sites are not just visually high-quality, but high-performing, discoverable, and accessible worldwide – a far cry from the dial-up days.

To create a 90s-style website in Framer, you can start with pre-built templates like Retro’98 or DeskTales. Get started with these, and other vintage designs, available in the Framer Marketplace. Then, when you’re ready, sign up for Framer to create your own site.

h1: How Framer sites use Traffic-aware Pre-Rendering
h3: Making the Framer Agent cheaper & faster
Selecting the unselectable, how we rebuilt block selection in Framer’s rich-text editor
How we pick translation models for Framer
p: How we’ve introduced Traffic-aware Pre-Rendering (TPR) to optimize pages on first visit, not per site on publish—faster results, same performance and SEO.

Framer sites are JavaScript apps built with React that render in the browser. For top speed, SEO, and AI, we pre-render pages on our servers. Then the browser or crawler can skip that work, leading to faster page loads. This is called server-side rendering.

In the past, we optimized every page on publish (often called Static Site Generation, SSG). But Framer now has more dynamic options like localization, A/B testing and many more upcoming. One page can turn into infinite page variations. Rendering all at once, even though the majority may not get visits before you publish again, would only delay how fast frequently visited and thus meaningful pages are optimized.

With TPR, we’re changing when we optimize pages. Instead of optimizing all pages on publish, we optimize each page the first time a user visits it. After that, the optimized version is stored in a cache until you publish a new version of your site.
This means the optimization step, which could take up to a minute for larger sites, is now essentially gone. It’s typically a second or less, no matter how many pages your site has.

Framer also knows your most popular pages from analytics. Based on the actual traffic of your site, we pre-render and optimize these pages before they get any visitors. This is done on every publish, which ensures we always pre-render the most meaningful pages based on the latest traffic data.

To make this work well, we made single page rendering very fast. Even if the first visit is less than 0.01% of visits, every visit counts. We did this by rethinking how we render sites and by adopting the state of the art web bundler Rolldown.
Gradual rollout of TPR has happened across all sites throughout October 2025. If you see the new status labels below, your site is using on-demand optimization:
Pre-Optimizing (was Optimizing): preparing dynamic optimization and optimizing top pages.
Ready (was Optimized): top pages are optimized; the rest are ready for dynamic optimization.
These are some advanced behaviors that technical people might want to know:

Right after a publish, all pages are new. If you use a tool (e.g. Lighthouse) that happens to test website performance right after a publish, results can look off. Aggregated performance scores like CrUX (used by Google search) are not affected, since the overwhelming majority of the visitors will get the optimized page.

If the page gets visited by a crawler that doesn’t run JavaScript, and that page wasn’t yet optimized, we’ll serve them the latest available optimized version instead. This makes dynamic optimization friendly for AI and social media bots.

As a direct result of the two points above, this change won’t impact SEO. Indirectly, it might help, since it allows us to pre-render more pages and introduce more dynamic options and page variations to further tailor your sites to your visitors.

If dynamic optimization runs into an error that could have a major impact on the page, we’ll send you an email. These are very rare. Optimization warnings, such as nested links or custom code bugs, have minimal impact, and only affect part of a page.
