h1: How to add hidden fields to forms for tracking
h3: When should I use hidden fields in Framer forms?
How do I add a hidden field to a form in Framer?
Can I use hidden fields in Framer to track UTM parameters automatically?
p: How to add hidden fields to forms for tracking
Learn how to include invisible data in form submissions for tracking and attribution.

Hidden fields let you include additional data in a form without users seeing or interacting with it. They’re useful when you want more context about a submission without changing the form’s appearance.
Hidden fields work well for tracking where submissions come from.

For example, if you have multiple landing pages with forms that all send data to the same webhook or Google Sheet, you can add a hidden text field with values like page-1 or page-2. This makes it easy to see which page generates the most submissions.

Note: Hidden fields in Framer don’t automatically bind to UTM parameters. UTM tracking for form submissions is available on Enterprise and Enterprise plans. You can also use a code override to pass UTM parameters into hidden fields if needed.
Follow these steps to add a hidden input field that will be included in form submissions without being visible to users.
Select your Form component on the canvas.
Add an Input field to the form.
Select the input field, then open the right-hand panel.
Set a Name for the input field. This name is what appears in the form submission.
Remove the label, if present, to keep the field fully invisible.

Note: Don’t hide the input using the Visible property. Invisible inputs are excluded from form submissions entirely. Always use the “Hidden” setting to ensure the field is included in the submitted data.

Hidden fields are useful for tracking where user submissions come from. For example, if you have multiple landing pages with forms that send data to the same Webhook or Google Sheet, you can track which page gets the most submissions by adding a hidden text field with values like “page 1” and “page 2.”

To add a hidden field in Framer, select your Form component, add an Input field to the form, select that input, then enable the Hidden property in the right-hand panel. Set a Name for the input field (this is what appears in submissions), and remove the label if present. Don’t hide it with the Visible property; use Hidden so the value is still included in submissions.

Hidden fields in Framer do not automatically bind to UTM parameters. UTM tracking for form submissions is available on Enterprise plans. You can also use a code override to pass UTM parameters into hidden fields.

p: How to use semantic tags for navigation and footers
Learn how to apply semantic HTML tags to navigation bars and footers in Framer to improve accessibility and site structure.

Semantic HTML tags help search engines and assistive technologies better understand your content. In Framer, you can apply these tags directly to frames to create a more accessible and well-structured website.
Use the nav tag to identify sections that contain primary navigation links.
Select the layer that contains your navigation links.

Use the footer tag to mark the footer section of your page.
Select the layer that serves as your footer.
Click the “Tag” dropdown and select footer.
This marks the frame as a footer, adding meaningful structure to your page.
Using semantic tags improves accessibility and SEO by making it easier for assistive technologies and search engines to interpret your site’s layout and purpose.

To apply the <nav> tag to your navigation bar, click on the layer containing your navigation links. In the properties panel, go to the “Accessibility” section, click the “Tag” dropdown, and select <nav>. This designates the frame as a navigation section, improving structure and accessibility.

To apply the <footer> tag, click on the layer serving as your footer. In the properties panel, under “Accessibility,” open the “Tag” dropdown and choose <footer>. This marks the frame as a footer, enhancing its semantic meaning.
Using these tags improves your site’s accessibility and SEO by making it easier for search engines and assistive technologies to interpret your content.

p: Learn how AI Style helps you guide the tone and voice of AI-powered translations in Framer.
AI Style lets you influence how Framer’s AI translates and presents your content, so it stays aligned with your brand voice.
Framer includes built-in localization tools that let you translate your site content using AI. AI Style builds on this by giving you more control over how those translations are written.

With AI Style, you provide a custom prompt that guides the AI’s tone, structure, and overall voice. This helps ensure translations feel intentional, consistent, and aligned with your brand, rather than generic or purely literal.
AI Style is especially helpful when you want to maintain a consistent voice across languages. Instead of accepting default translations, you can shape how the AI interprets and rewrites your content.
Keeping a consistent brand tone across all locales
Matching translations to your design or creative direction
Adapting language for specific audiences, such as technical, friendly, or marketing-focused readers
AI Style acts as creative direction for the AI. You describe how the AI should “think” when translating your content, and Framer applies that guidance across your localized text.
For example, you might ask the AI to:
Write in a friendly and conversational tone
Use a concise, minimalist writing style
Adapt wording for a younger or more playful audience
The clearer your prompt, the more accurately the AI can reflect your intended style.

/guides/webflow-to-framer-seo/.title: Webflow to Framer SEO migration checklist and guide
/guides/webflow-to-framer-seo/.description: Protect SEO during a Webflow-to-Framer migration with URL mapping, redirects, metadata, structured data, testing, and Search Console monitoring.
h3: Does moving from Webflow to Framer hurt SEO?
Does Framer create a sitemap and robots.txt?
Should I use Google’s Change of Address tool?
h4: 3. Save metadata and a performance baseline
p: Moving from Webflow to Framer does not need to reduce search visibility. Keep valuable URLs and content stable, map every changed path, recreate metadata and structured data, and verify the live site in Search Console. Separate the platform change from unnecessary content or URL changes so problems are easier to diagnose. The step-by-step migration guide covers the rest of the move.

Crawl all static, CMS, localized, utility, and campaign routes. Record each URL’s status, canonical, indexability, title, description, headings, internal links, and content type. Include links inside Webflow rich-text fields.

Give every source URL one outcome: keep, redirect, merge, or remove. Keep useful paths and CMS slugs unchanged where possible. Include existing Webflow redirect destinations so the new setup does not create chains.

Export titles, descriptions, social metadata, canonicals, structured data, noindex rules, localized alternatives, and image alt text. Save Search Console clicks, impressions, queries, pages, conversions, and Core Web Vitals so you can compare the result after launch.

Preserve page paths, CMS slugs, localized routes, headings, useful copy, and internal-link relationships unless there is a clear reason to change them. Update rich-text links and re-host important Webflow CDN assets in Framer.
Redirect only changed or removed URLs. Send each source URL directly to the closest relevant destination and avoid chains, loops, and broad redirects to the homepage.

Framer supports exact, wildcard, capture-group, and named-parameter redirects. When importing redirects in bulk, use a CSV with from and to columns. Entries that match an existing from path update that redirect, while other existing redirects remain unchanged. If the domain changes, keep the old domain configured so it can forward requests. See Framer’s bulk redirect import guide.

Set a unique title, description, social preview, canonical, and search visibility for each important page and CMS template. Recreate useful JSON-LD with custom code and validate what appears on the published page.

Use structured data that matches visible content. FAQ content can make the page easier to understand, but FAQ rich results in Google are generally limited to authoritative government and health sites.

Map each Webflow locale to the correct Framer route. Check language alternatives, canonicals, internal links, localized CMS slugs, noindex settings, sitemap.xml, and robots.txt. Framer automatically generates a sitemap and robots.txt for published sites.

Test representative static, CMS, localized, and utility URLs. Check metadata, canonicals, structured data, redirects, internal links, mobile rendering, forms, analytics, the 404 page, sitemap.xml, and robots.txt.

Repeat the checks on the production domain after DNS and SSL are active. If the domain or subdomain changes, verify both the old and new properties in Search Console before launch and keep a verification method that survives the cutover. Submit the Framer sitemap in Search Console and inspect important URLs. Use Google’s Change of Address tool only when the domain or subdomain changes, not for a platform-only move on the same domain.

Monitor crawl errors, indexing, canonicals, traffic, conversions, and important rankings. Fix 404s, redirect chains, blocked pages, incorrect canonicals, missing metadata, and broken internal links by cause. Keep redirects for as long as possible, generally at least one year, following Google’s site-move guidance.

Not by itself. The main risks come from changing URLs, removing useful content, losing metadata or structured data, breaking internal links, or missing redirects. Keeping those signals stable and testing the production site reduces the risk.
No. If the domain and full path stay the same, the page can keep serving at that URL. Add a redirect only when the source URL changes or is intentionally removed.

Yes. Framer generates sitemap.xml and robots.txt for published sites. Verify both files after launch and submit the sitemap in Search Console. Framer also serves optimized pages as structured markdown to supported AI agents, which you can preview by adding ?md to a published URL. See Make your site readable by AI agents.
Use it when the migration changes the domain or subdomain. Do not use it for a move from Webflow to Framer that keeps the same domain.
Finish with the Webflow to Framer migration checklist.

/guides/webflow-to-framer-why-teams-swit.title: Why teams migrate from Webflow to Framer: Key reasons
/guides/webflow-to-framer-why-teams-swit.description: Learn why teams migrate from Webflow to Framer for faster publishing, simpler maintenance, design control, CMS workflows, and fewer handoffs.
h2: Why do teams move from Webflow to Framer?
h3: 3. A shorter path from Figma to production
p: Teams usually move from Webflow to Framer when the website needs to be easier for design and marketing to own. The strongest reasons are faster publishing, a simpler design system, a shorter path from Figma to production, and a lower workflow cost. The right choice still depends on the site’s CMS, integrations, and custom behavior. See the step-by-step migration guide to evaluate the work.

Framer lets designers and marketers build, edit, review, and publish in the same visual environment. This can reduce handoffs for landing pages, campaigns, CMS content, and routine site updates while still supporting permissions and review workflows for larger teams.

Large Webflow projects can become difficult to maintain when class combinations, overrides, and one-off patterns accumulate. Framer uses components, variants, text and color styles, and variables instead of Webflow’s class hierarchy. A migration is an opportunity to consolidate repeated patterns and remove unused styling.

Framer’s canvas and component model feel familiar to many Figma users. Designers can build production pages more directly, test responsive layouts and interactions in place, and reduce the translation work between design and implementation.

The relevant cost is not only the platform plan. Include the time spent translating designs, maintaining the design system, waiting for developer support, managing integrations, and fixing regressions. Framer can reduce that overhead for design-led marketing sites, although migration and specialist work still need a realistic budget.

Framer’s Agent and External Agents can help rebuild pages, create or import CMS content, add redirects, and review a migration. They are useful for repetitive work, but current migration results still need human review for exact assets, responsive layouts, interactions, content, forms, and SEO. See Migrating with Agents.
These examples show different migration goals. Treat the outcomes as context, not as guarantees for every site.

LoopsLoops wanted routine updates and launches to move faster. After moving from Webflow, the team brought its blog, changelog, and template marketplace into Framer and reduced its reliance on developer support.

BountiBounti rebuilt its Webflow site in Framer with localization, structured CMS content, and an SEO-focused architecture. The company reports a better visitor experience, a higher demo-booking conversion rate, and fewer engineering bottlenecks.

bunqbunq moved its main marketing site from Webflow to Framer and operates it across multiple locales. The project shows the importance of dedicated review for localization, consent, analytics, CMS content, and launch planning on a large multilingual site.
A Framer Expert can help plan the migration, rebuild the design system, move CMS content, and prepare the site for launch.

p: Link unfurling is the process of expanding a pasted URL into a rich preview card. Apps fetch page metadata, choose a title and image, and render the result inline. A link preview checker helps predict what that unfurled link will show.

/dictionary/google-snippet.title: Google Snippet: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/google-snippet.description: Learn what Google Snippet means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A Google snippet is the page preview shown in Google search results. It usually includes a title, URL, and description selected from metadata or page content. Use Link Preview to check the metadata that can influence how the snippet reads.

/dictionary/url-unfurling.title: URL Unfurling: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/url-unfurling.description: Learn what URL Unfurling means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: URL unfurling is the metadata-driven expansion of a web address into a readable preview. It is common in Slack, messaging apps, social feeds, and collaboration tools. Use Link Preview to inspect the metadata that may be used during unfurling.

/dictionary/meta-tag-generator.title: Meta Tag Generator: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/meta-tag-generator.description: Learn what Meta Tag Generator means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A meta tag generator is a tool or workflow for creating metadata values before publishing a page. It helps write titles, descriptions, Open Graph values, and social preview text. After generating metadata, use a meta tag checker to verify the live result.

/dictionary/social-image.title: Social Image: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/social-image.description: Learn what Social Image means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A social image is the image used in link previews on social platforms, messaging apps, and collaboration tools. It often comes from the Open Graph image field. Preview the social image to make sure it stays legible at card sizes.

/dictionary/meta-tag-checker.title: Meta Tag Checker: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/meta-tag-checker.description: Learn what Meta Tag Checker means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A meta tag checker is a tool that audits the metadata published on a URL. It can inspect title tags, meta descriptions, Open Graph tags, Twitter Card metadata, favicons, canonical URLs, and preview images. Link Preview is built for this type of check.

/dictionary/meta-title.title: Meta Title: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/meta-title.description: Learn what Meta Title means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A meta title is the page title used by search engines, browsers, and many link preview surfaces. It often comes from the title tag or a platform-specific title field. A meta tag checker helps confirm the title is specific, readable, and not truncated.

/dictionary/og-image-checker.title: OG Image Checker: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/og-image-checker.description: Learn what OG Image Checker means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: An OG image checker is a tool for verifying that an Open Graph preview image loads, crops, and communicates correctly. It helps catch missing images, poor aspect ratios, and vague preview artwork. Link Preview includes OG image checking as part of its preview workflow.

/dictionary/x-preview-card.title: X Preview Card: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/x-preview-card.description: Learn what X Preview Card means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: An X preview card is the link card displayed by X when a URL includes supported Twitter Card metadata. It usually shows a title, description, image, and source domain. Check the preview with Link Preview before sharing campaign or launch links.

/dictionary/og-image.title: OG Image: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/og-image.description: Learn what OG Image means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: An OG image is the preview image used by Open Graph cards when a page is shared. It should communicate the page topic clearly even when cropped or compressed. Use an OG image checker to confirm the image loads and displays well.

/dictionary/open-graph-checker.title: Open Graph Checker: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/open-graph-checker.description: Learn what Open Graph Checker means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: An Open Graph checker is a tool that reads a page’s Open Graph metadata and previews the resulting share card. It checks fields like OG title, OG description, OG image, URL, and favicon. This Open Graph checker can help validate those values before a page is shared.

/dictionary/open-graph-tags.title: Open Graph Tags: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/open-graph-tags.description: Learn what Open Graph Tags means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Open Graph tags are metadata fields that control how a page appears when shared on platforms that support Open Graph. Common tags include og:title, og:description, og:image, and og:url. A meta tag checker can show whether those tags are present and useful.

/dictionary/shared-link-preview.title: Shared Link Preview: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/shared-link-preview.description: Learn what Shared Link Preview means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A shared link preview is the title, description, image, and domain shown when a link is pasted into another product. Strong previews make links feel trustworthy and clickable. Use Link Preview to inspect how a shared link may appear before launch.

/dictionary/social-card.title: Social Card: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/social-card.description: Learn what Social Card means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A social card is the compact preview block that represents a shared URL on social platforms and messaging apps. It typically uses Open Graph or Twitter Card metadata to display a title, description, image, and domain. Preview the card with a social card checker before sharing important pages.

/dictionary/url-preview.title: URL Preview: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/url-preview.description: Learn what URL Preview means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A URL preview is the rendered summary of a web address shown before someone opens the link. It can appear in search results, Slack, WhatsApp, LinkedIn, X, and other surfaces. A URL preview tool helps verify the metadata that powers that summary.

/dictionary/social-preview.title: Social Preview: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/social-preview.description: Learn what Social Preview means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A social preview is the visual card generated when a page is shared on social networks, chat apps, or collaboration tools. It helps people understand the page before clicking. Testing the social preview helps catch missing images, weak titles, and generic descriptions.

/dictionary/link-preview.title: Link Preview: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/link-preview.description: Learn what Link Preview means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A link preview is the card-like summary of a URL shown when a page is shared in search, social apps, messaging tools, and collaboration platforms. It usually combines a title, description, image, favicon, and destination URL. Use a link preview checker to confirm the shared card is clear before publishing.

/dictionary/link-preview-checker.title: Link Preview Checker: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/link-preview-checker.description: Learn what Link Preview Checker means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: A link preview checker is a tool for testing how a URL appears when shared across social, search, and messaging surfaces. It reads metadata such as title tags, meta descriptions, Open Graph tags, Twitter cards, favicons, and preview images. Link Preview is one example of this workflow.

/dictionary/seo-ready.title: SEO Ready: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/seo-ready.description: Learn what SEO Ready means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, SEO-ready sites combine editable metadata, clean page structure, fast loading, responsive layouts, and publishing tools that help pages perform well in search.

A free Google tool providing insights into how your site appears in search results, including impressions, clicks, and indexing issues. Search Console alerts you to problems and validates fixes, essential for SEO monitoring. Verify your Framer site in Search Console to track search performance.

A platform for buying, selling, or sharing design resources, templates, and assets within a tool's ecosystem. Marketplaces accelerate projects by providing ready-made solutions and components. Browse Framer's marketplace for templates, components, and inspiration.

Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is the practice of improving a site’s visibility in search results through technical quality, relevant content, and authority signals. Strong SEO combines crawlability, performance, metadata, internal linking, and useful content. Framer supports SEO with clean markup, metadata controls, and sitemap generation.

An incoming hyperlink from another website pointing to your site, considered a vote of confidence by search engines. Quality backlinks from reputable sites significantly boost SEO by signaling that your content is valuable and trustworthy. Building backlinks requires creating shareable content, guest posting, and developing relationships with relevant publications in your industry.

Domain Authority (DA) is a third-party metric (commonly from Moz) that estimates how likely a domain is to rank. It is not a Google ranking score or an official search-engine metric. Treat it as a comparative benchmark, not a direct ranking factor.

/dictionary/svg-optimization.title: SVG Optimization: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/svg-optimization.description: Learn what SVG Optimization means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, optimized SVGs help maintain crisp visuals while reducing unnecessary markup, file size, and rendering cost on published pages.

The process of reducing image file sizes while maintaining acceptable visual quality for faster page loads. Optimized images can be 10x smaller than originals without noticeable quality loss, dramatically improving performance. Framer automatically optimizes uploaded images, converting to efficient formats like WebP where supported.

A measure of how quickly page content loads and becomes interactive, influenced by file sizes, server response, and code efficiency. Google uses page speed as a ranking factor, making optimization both a UX and SEO concern. Framer’s infrastructure and automatic optimizations help achieve fast page speeds.

/dictionary/resource-culling.title: Resource Culling: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/resource-culling.description: Learn what Resource Culling means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, resource culling supports leaner pages by keeping unnecessary media, scripts, and interface resources out of the critical loading path.
In Framer, code splitting supports faster initial loads by avoiding unnecessary JavaScript on first view and loading additional code only when it becomes relevant.

/dictionary/font-subsetting.title: Font Subsetting: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/font-subsetting.description: Learn what Font Subsetting means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, font subsetting can improve page speed by minimizing font downloads while preserving the typography needed for the published site.

A variable font containing multiple weights, widths, or styles in a single file, enabling smooth interpolation between values. Variable fonts reduce file downloads while offering greater typographic flexibility. Use variable fonts for performance benefits and fluid typography that responds to user preferences.

/dictionary/responsive-images.title: Responsive Images: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/responsive-images.description: Learn what Responsive Images means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, responsive images help pages load faster and look sharp by serving suitable image sizes instead of forcing every visitor to download oversized assets.

A standalone page designed for a specific marketing goal, typically with focused messaging and a single call to action. Unlike general website pages, landing pages minimize distractions to maximize conversions. Test landing page variations systematically—small changes in headlines, images, or CTAs can significantly impact results.

The smallest unit of a digital display, a single point of color that combines with millions of others to form images. Understanding pixel dimensions helps you provide appropriate image sizes for different devices. Retina displays pack more pixels into the same space, requiring higher-resolution images for sharp display.

An image that adapts to different screen sizes and resolutions, serving appropriately sized versions for each context. Responsive images improve performance by avoiding unnecessarily large downloads on small screens. Framer handles responsive images automatically, serving optimized versions.

The process of reducing file sizes by removing redundant data, making assets faster to download and cheaper to serve. Image compression can reduce file sizes by 50-80% with minimal visual quality loss using formats like WebP. Framer automatically optimizes images for web delivery while preserving quality where it matters most.

Dots Per Inch—a measure of print resolution indicating how many ink dots fit in one inch, affecting print quality and file size. Higher DPI produces sharper prints but larger files. For web, focus on PPI (pixels per inch) and responsive images rather than DPI.
In Framer workflows, exportable layers help teams move graphics, images, and design assets between site production, marketing, and documentation needs.

In Framer, resource culling supports leaner pages by keeping unnecessary media, scripts, and interface resources out of the critical loading path.

p: In Framer, instant navigation helps multi-page sites feel faster by reducing delay between clicks and page changes, especially when paired with preloading and optimized routes.

The system of links and menus that helps users find content and move through a website. Good navigation is consistent, clearly labeled, and reflects user mental models about site structure. Test navigation with real users to ensure your labels and organization make sense to your audience.
Animated transitions between page or state views that preserve continuity as content changes. View transitions can make navigation feel smoother and reduce abrupt visual jumps.
In Framer, route prefetching helps visitors move between pages with less waiting by preparing linked destinations before they are clicked.

/dictionary/global-cdn.title: Global CDN: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/global-cdn.description: Learn what Global CDN means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer uses global delivery infrastructure to help pages, images, scripts, and assets reach visitors quickly across regions, improving perceived speed and reliability.

Content Delivery Network—a distributed network of servers that delivers web content from locations geographically closest to each visitor. CDNs dramatically reduce latency and load times for global audiences while providing redundancy if one server fails. Framer hosts all sites on a global CDN automatically, ensuring fast performance worldwide without additional configuration.

A library of free, open-source web fonts hosted by Google with global CDN delivery for fast loading. Google Fonts simplifies typography with easy embedding and wide browser support. Framer integrates Google Fonts directly, making them available without additional configuration.

The service that stores website files and serves them to visitors over the internet. Reliable hosting affects site speed, uptime, and security—poor hosting can undermine great design. Framer includes premium hosting on a global CDN with automatic SSL, eliminating the need for separate hosting configuration.

A distributed network of servers that delivers web content from locations geographically closest to each visitor, reducing latency and improving load times. CDNs also provide redundancy and protection against traffic spikes or server failures. Framer hosts all sites on a global CDN automatically for optimal worldwide performance.

/dictionary/edge-caching.title: Edge Caching: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/edge-caching.description: Learn what Edge Caching means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, edge caching improves performance by reducing distance and server work for published pages and assets, helping sites respond quickly around the world.

Temporary storage that keeps copies of assets so repeat visits load faster and consume less bandwidth. Effective caching can significantly improve page-load performance for returning users. CDNs and browser cache policies work together to deliver assets efficiently.

The process of storing frequently accessed data in temporary storage for faster retrieval on subsequent requests. Browser caching stores assets locally while server caching reduces database queries and processing time. Understanding caching helps troubleshoot why changes don't appear immediately—you may need to clear cache or wait for CDN propagation.

Metadata sent with HTTP requests and responses that controls behavior such as caching, security policies, and content handling. Common examples include Cache-Control, Content-Security-Policy, and Strict-Transport-Security.
In Framer, squircle corner styling can make cards, buttons, and panels feel more refined by blending geometric structure with a softer edge profile.

/dictionary/team-workspaces.description: Learn what Team workspaces means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, team workspaces give groups a shared place to manage sites, collaborate on designs, and keep ownership clear across projects.

A shared environment in Framer where teams organize projects, manage billing, and control member access. Workspaces make it easier to collaborate across multiple sites with centralized settings and permissions. See Organizations, Workspaces, and Folders.
A plugin designed for workspace-level workflows such as governance, automation, or team operations across multiple projects. Workspace plugins extend Framer beyond single-file editing tasks.
Framer ownership transfer helps teams hand off sites cleanly between collaborators, clients, or workspaces while preserving project structure and access.

/dictionary/custom-domains.title: Custom domains: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/custom-domains.description: Learn what Custom domains means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer custom domains let teams publish production websites on their own domain, keeping collaboration, hosting, and launch workflows in one place.

A personalized web address like yourbrand.com instead of a platform-provided subdomain. Custom domains are essential for professional branding and improve trustworthiness with visitors. Framer supports custom domains with automatic SSL certificate provisioning and straightforward DNS configuration.

Domain Name System—the internet’s phone book that translates human-readable domain names into numerical IP addresses computers use. DNS propagation can take 24-48 hours when pointing a domain to new hosting, though it often completes much faster. Proper DNS configuration is essential for connecting custom domains to your Framer site.

The human-readable address of a website that users type in browsers, translating to numerical IP addresses behind the scenes. Choose domain names that are memorable, brandable, and relevant to your content. Shorter domains are generally easier to remember and type correctly.

A registrar is the company that manages domain registration, renewals, and DNS control for your domain name. Choose a reliable registrar with clear pricing, DNS tooling, and strong support. Common options include Namecheap, Cloudflare Registrar, and Squarespace Domains. See Is Framer a domain registrar?.

A server setup that forwards incoming requests to another origin while keeping your public domain unchanged. Reverse proxies are used for migrations, custom routing, security policies, and integrating Framer with existing infrastructure. See How to self host using a reverse proxy.
Framer plugins help teams add new capabilities to the editor, automate repetitive work, and connect design workflows to external services without leaving the project.

/dictionary/share-for-review.title: Share for review: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/share-for-review.description: Learn what Share for review means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, review sharing helps teams gather comments, approvals, and direction on a live preview or project state before changes go public.

A pre-production environment used to review and test changes before they go live. Staging helps teams validate content, layout, and behavior safely before publishing to the production site. See Publishing your Framer website.
A timeline of saved project states that allows you to review, compare, and restore earlier versions. Version history reduces risk when iterating by making rollbacks straightforward.
A Publish Staging URL is a temporary or preview deployment address that allows teams to validate content and design before publishing to production.
Site Preview is a non-production view of a site used to test design, content, and interactions before a production publish.
A branch preview is a shareable version of work on a branch, used to review changes before merging or publishing them live.
In collaborative Framer workflows, branch preview helps teams move faster without losing control of structure, content, performance, or editable design details.
Framer comments keep feedback connected to the exact design context, helping teams review pages, resolve decisions, and collaborate without scattering notes across tools.

/dictionary/auto-save.title: Auto-save: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/auto-save.description: Learn what Auto-save means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer auto-save protects design progress while teams edit pages, components, and content, making collaboration faster and reducing the risk of losing work.

A rotating display of multiple pieces of content within a single space, allowing users to navigate through items using arrows or swipe gestures. While carousels save space, studies show users often miss content beyond the first slide—consider whether a grid might be more effective. If using carousels, ensure clear navigation indicators and consider auto-play carefully.
In Framer, guest editors make it easier to bring clients, contractors, or teammates into a specific project while keeping broader workspace access controlled.

/dictionary/masks.title: Masks: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/masks.description: Learn what Masks means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer masks help designers create image treatments, reveal effects, soft fades, and graphic compositions without flattening the work into static assets.

Segment Anything Model (SAM) produces masks from points, boxes, or text-like prompts for rapid object selection. It underpins modern Image Segmentation workflows and improves control in Reference Image editing.

Image Segmentation partitions an image into labeled regions to isolate objects or areas for editing. It is core to Segment Anything Model (SAM) workflows and precision operations like Generative Fill.
Framer’s vector tools let designers craft visual assets in place, keeping illustrations, masks, and interface details editable alongside the rest of the site.

/dictionary/multiplayer-cursors.title: Multiplayer cursors: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/multiplayer-cursors.description: Learn what Multiplayer cursors means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, multiplayer cursors make collaboration feel immediate by showing teammates’ presence on the canvas, helping teams design together without losing context.

The visual indicator showing the mouse position on screen, which changes shape to indicate possible interactions. Custom cursors can reinforce branding and provide feedback about interactive elements. In Framer, the cursor becomes contextual tools for placing elements and manipulating the canvas during design.
Branch-aware cursors show collaborators in the correct branch context, so teams can review and edit without confusing separate versions of a project.
In collaborative Framer workflows, branch-aware cursors helps teams move faster without losing control of structure, content, performance, or editable design details.
Framer comments keep feedback connected to the exact design context, helping teams review pages, resolve decisions, and collaborate without scattering notes across tools.
In Framer, guest editors make it easier to bring clients, contractors, or teammates into a specific project while keeping broader workspace access controlled.

/dictionary/svg-animations.title: SVG animations: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/svg-animations.description: Learn what SVG animations means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, SVG animations can add lightweight motion to icons, illustrations, logos, and interface details while keeping visuals crisp at any size.

Any way users engage with your interface, from clicks and hovers to scrolls and gestures. Well-designed interactions feel responsive and intuitive while providing clear feedback. Framer enables complex interactions through triggers, animations, and state changes without coding.

An animation tool and runtime for creating interactive graphics that respond to user input in real time. Rive animations are lightweight and highly interactive, enabling complex state-driven animations. Import Rive files for sophisticated interactive elements.

Scalable Vector Graphics—an image format using mathematical paths instead of pixels, staying crisp at any size. SVGs are perfect for logos, icons, and illustrations that need to scale across different screen sizes and densities. Framer supports SVG import and handles them optimally for web delivery.
In Framer, optimized SVGs help maintain crisp visuals while reducing unnecessary markup, file size, and rendering cost on published pages.

/dictionary/custom-cursor.title: Custom cursor: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/custom-cursor.description: Learn what Custom cursor means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer custom cursors can add interaction feedback, brand personality, or contextual hints while visitors move through highly designed pages.

The visual indicator showing the mouse position on screen, which changes shape to indicate possible interactions. Custom cursors can reinforce branding and provide feedback about interactive elements. In Framer, the cursor becomes contextual tools for placing elements and manipulating the canvas during design.

The visual appearance of an element when a user's cursor is positioned over it, providing feedback and indicating interactivity. Hover states are essential for buttons, links, and clickable elements—without them, users can't tell what's interactive. Remember that hover doesn't exist on touch devices, so don't rely on it for essential information.

/dictionary/truncation.title: Truncation: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/truncation.description: Learn what Truncation means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, truncation is useful for cards, lists, and CMS-driven content where titles or descriptions may vary in length but the layout should remain aligned.

/dictionary/squircle-corners.title: Squircle corners: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/squircle-corners.description: Learn what Squircle corners means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, squircle corner styling can make cards, buttons, and panels feel more refined by blending geometric structure with a softer edge profile.

/dictionary/link-styles.title: Link styles: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/link-styles.description: Learn what Link styles means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer link styles keep navigation, inline links, and active states consistent, so interactive text feels intentional across pages and CMS content.

A family of fonts sharing consistent design characteristics, such as Helvetica or Inter, containing multiple weights and styles. Choose typefaces that reflect brand personality while maintaining readability. Limit to 2-3 typefaces per project for cohesion.

A design approach where digital interfaces mimic real-world objects with realistic textures, shadows, and materials. Skeuomorphism provides familiar metaphors but has largely given way to flatter design styles. Some skeuomorphic elements persist where real-world familiarity aids understanding.
A Font Family is a grouped collection of type styles and weights designed with consistent visual DNA for cohesive typography systems.

/dictionary/selection-color.title: Selection color: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/selection-color.description: Learn what Selection color means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer selection colors let teams align the small details of browser interaction with the site’s visual system, reinforcing brand polish even in native behaviors.

The study of how colors interact, combine, and influence perception, guiding designers in creating harmonious palettes that evoke specific emotions. Understanding complementary, analogous, and triadic color relationships helps create visually balanced designs. Apply color theory to establish brand moods and guide user attention to key elements.

The perceived heaviness of an element based on size, color, contrast, and complexity, affecting visual balance. Understanding visual weight helps create balanced compositions without symmetry. Use visual weight to guide attention and establish hierarchy.

The arrangement of elements to show their order of importance through size, color, contrast, and position. Strong hierarchy guides users through content in the intended order and highlights key actions. Squint at your design—hierarchy issues become obvious when details blur.
Analogous Colors are color combinations made from adjacent hues on the color wheel, often used to create cohesive and low-contrast visual systems.
A HEX Value is a web color notation like #RRGGBB used in CSS and design tools to represent exact RGB color values.

/dictionary/text-balance.title: Text balance: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/text-balance.description: Learn what Text balance means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, balanced text can make headlines and supporting copy feel more intentional across screen sizes by reducing awkward single-word lines.

An interactive element that collects user input through fields like text boxes, dropdowns, and checkboxes. Well-designed forms balance collecting necessary information with respecting user time and effort. Keep forms short, use clear labels, provide helpful validation messages, and consider progressive disclosure for complex forms.

The uniform adjustment of space between all characters in a word or block of text, also called tracking. Increased letter spacing can improve readability for uppercase text and small sizes. Avoid negative letter spacing in body text as it impairs readability.

The vertical space allocated to each line of text, affecting readability and overall text block appearance. Proper line height prevents cramped or overly loose text—typically 1.4-1.6 for body copy. Adjust line height proportionally with font size for consistent rhythm.

Written content displayed on web pages, the primary means of communicating information to visitors. Quality text content is essential for engagement, SEO, and accessibility. Structure text with headings, short paragraphs, and scannable formatting.

The adjustment of space between individual letter pairs to achieve visually balanced text, particularly important in headlines and logos. Poor kerning creates awkward gaps or collisions that undermine professional appearance. Pay special attention to problematic pairs like AV, To, and We where mechanical spacing looks wrong.

The height of lowercase letters in a typeface, measured using the letter ‘x’, affecting perceived size and readability. Fonts with larger x-heights appear larger and more readable at small sizes. Consider x-height when selecting fonts for body text.

/dictionary/layout-templates.title: Layout templates: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/layout-templates.description: Learn what Layout templates means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer layout templates help teams reuse global structure across pages, keeping navigation, footers, and shared layout behavior consistent while each page keeps its own content.

A CSS layout method that removes an element from the normal document flow and positions it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor. This technique is useful for overlays, badges, and decorative elements that need precise placement regardless of surrounding content. Use sparingly, as absolutely positioned elements don’t affect the layout of other elements and can cause overlap issues on different screen sizes.

The arrangement of visual elements on a page, establishing structure, hierarchy, and flow of information. Good layout guides the eye naturally through content while creating visual harmony. Consider reading patterns—users typically scan in F or Z patterns on text-heavy pages.

The space outside an element’s border, creating separation from neighboring elements. Margin helps control rhythm and spacing between blocks of content. In Framer, use spacing controls and layoutauto layout gap for consistent, predictable layout behavior.

Positioning that keeps an element in normal document flow while allowing offset adjustments from its default location. It is useful for minor visual nudges and for establishing a positioning context for absolutely positioned children. Prefer layout tools for larger structural alignment.

Creating a new project based on an existing template or shared design, inheriting structure while enabling customization. Remixing accelerates projects by building on proven foundations. Explore Framer's community for remixable templates and components.

A pre-designed, reusable starting point containing layout structure, styles, and often placeholder content. Templates accelerate projects by providing tested foundations rather than starting from scratch. Framer offers professional templates for common site types that can be fully customized.

/dictionary/text-decoration.title: Text decoration: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/text-decoration.description: Learn what Text decoration means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer text decoration helps designers style links, emphasis, and editorial details while keeping type treatments consistent across a site.

The adjustment of space between individual letter pairs to achieve visually balanced text, particularly important in headlines and logos. Poor kerning creates awkward gaps or collisions that undermine professional appearance. Pay special attention to problematic pairs like AV, To, and We where mechanical spacing looks wrong.
Justified text alignment stretches line spacing so text aligns on both margins, improving visual structure but requiring careful spacing control.
Readability describes how comfortably users can consume written content, influenced by typography, line length, spacing, and visual contrast.
Sans Serif refers to letterforms without small finishing strokes, commonly chosen for modern, legible screen typography.
Serif typefaces include decorative terminal strokes that can convey tradition, credibility, and reading comfort in long-form text.
In Framer, balanced text can make headlines and supporting copy feel more intentional across screen sizes by reducing awkward single-word lines.

/dictionary/export-layers.title: Export layers: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/export-layers.description: Learn what Export layers means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer workflows, exportable layers help teams move graphics, images, and design assets between site production, marketing, and documentation needs.

An element in the design stack that can be positioned above or below other elements, controlling visual overlap. Layers enable complex compositions with overlapping elements and effects. Manage layer order in Framer's left sidebar or use z-index for precise control.
In Framer, Expert access can help teams move faster by getting guidance on design, implementation, migration, or launch decisions from experienced Framer professionals.

/dictionary/comments.title: Comments: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/comments.description: Learn what Comments means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer comments keep feedback connected to the exact design context, helping teams review pages, resolve decisions, and collaborate without scattering notes across tools.

The process of removing unnecessary characters from code—whitespace, comments, line breaks—to reduce file size. Minification speeds up loading without changing functionality, typically applied to CSS and JavaScript. Framer automatically minifies code for production deployment.

Real-time or on-demand suggestions provided by an AI model as a developer types, ranging from single-word completions to entire function bodies. Modern tools like GitHub Copilot and Cursor use large language models to infer intent from surrounding code and comments. Code completion reduces keystrokes, surfaces patterns, and helps developers stay in flow—while requiring judgment about whether suggestions are correct and appropriate.
In Framer, multiplayer cursors make collaboration feel immediate by showing teammates’ presence on the canvas, helping teams design together without losing context.

p: Framer tickers can add motion to marquees, partner logos, feature labels, and repeated content while preserving a clean editable layout.

/dictionary/sticky-positioning.title: Sticky positioning: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/sticky-positioning.description: Learn what Sticky positioning means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: In Framer, sticky positioning is useful for sidebars, navigation aids, comparison panels, and storytelling layouts where one element should remain visible during part of the scroll.

A CSS layout method that removes an element from the normal document flow and positions it relative to its nearest positioned ancestor. This technique is useful for overlays, badges, and decorative elements that need precise placement regardless of surrounding content. Use sparingly, as absolutely positioned elements don’t affect the layout of other elements and can cause overlap issues on different screen sizes.

A positioning method that anchors elements relative to the browser viewport, keeping them visible during scrolling. Fixed elements are useful for sticky navigation, floating action buttons, and persistent calls to action. Use fixed positioning sparingly to avoid blocking content and reducing usable space.

The CSS property determining how an element is placed in the document flow—static, relative, absolute, fixed, or sticky. Understanding positioning is essential for creating overlays, sticky elements, and complex layouts. Framer provides visual controls for common positioning patterns.

Positioning that keeps an element in normal document flow while allowing offset adjustments from its default location. It is useful for minor visual nudges and for establishing a positioning context for absolutely positioned children. Prefer layout tools for larger structural alignment.

A hybrid positioning method where elements behave normally until reaching a scroll threshold, then fix in place. Sticky positioning creates headers that stay visible during scrolling within their container. Use sticky for navigation, sidebar elements, and persistent calls to action.

A navigation bar that remains fixed at the top of the viewport as users scroll down the page. Sticky navigation keeps primary actions accessible without scrolling back up. Ensure sticky elements don't consume too much screen space on mobile.

/dictionary/p3-colors.title: P3 colors: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/p3-colors.description: Learn what P3 colors means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer designs can use wide-gamut color values for more vivid accents and gradients on supported displays, helping modern sites feel brighter and more refined.

The study of how colors interact, combine, and influence perception, guiding designers in creating harmonious palettes that evoke specific emotions. Understanding complementary, analogous, and triadic color relationships helps create visually balanced designs. Apply color theory to establish brand moods and guide user attention to key elements.

A visual collage of images, colors, typography, and textures capturing the intended look and feel of a project. Mood boards align stakeholders on aesthetic direction before detailed design begins. Create mood boards to explore and communicate design concepts efficiently.

Named values storing design decisions like colors, spacing, and typography, enabling systematic design across platforms. Tokens create a single source of truth that can be translated to different implementation contexts. In Framer, variables serve as design tokens for colors, numbers, and responsive values.

Adjusting element positions based on visual perception rather than mathematical precision, making designs feel balanced. Optical alignment acknowledges that geometric centering doesn't always look centered to human eyes. Fine-tune alignments manually when mathematical precision creates visual imbalance.
Analogous Colors are color combinations made from adjacent hues on the color wheel, often used to create cohesive and low-contrast visual systems.
Framer selection colors let teams align the small details of browser interaction with the site’s visual system, reinforcing brand polish even in native behaviors.

/dictionary/auto-sizing.title: Auto sizing: Definition, Examples, and Framer Context
/dictionary/auto-sizing.description: Learn what Auto sizing means, why it matters in web design, and how it applies when building with Framer.
p: Framer auto sizing keeps cards, buttons, sections, and text groups flexible, making responsive layouts easier to maintain as content changes.

The fundamental container element in Framer that holds content and defines boundaries for layout, sizing, and visual properties. Frames are the building blocks of every Framer design, from tiny icons to full page layouts. Unlike groups, frames have their own properties and can contain responsive layouts and effects.

A mathematical proportion of approximately 1:1.618 found throughout nature and art, often used to create aesthetically pleasing layouts. The golden ratio can guide element sizing, spacing, and composition decisions. While not a strict rule, it provides a starting point for harmonious proportions.

/developers/faq.title: Framer Developers: FAQ
h4: Should I use code in Framer?
Is Framer a full blown developer platform?
What happens if I make a bug in my custom code?
My custom code isn’t working as expected, can you help me debug?
Can I share my code components across projects?
Can I import Framer components into my React application directly?
Should I use external code libraries with Framer?
Should I add state management to let components communicate?
Should I use code to integrate tokens or build design systems for my team?
p: Framer is a site builder that doesn’t require code. Code in Framer is a way to extend the application beyond that standard (very extensive) functionality.You should use code in Framer if you are comfortable with React and JavaScript and need to add something dynamic to your website that Framer cannot provide out of the box, like a menu login button or a metric integration.

Can it help me write code? No. Framer uses code as an escape hatch to extend capabilities to for example add small dynamic parts to a site. If your project needs a lot of logic and components we advise to create a normal React application instead.

Code in Framer shares the runtime and dom with everything else. That means that you can do anything, but also that subtle bugs can break your entire site. In short, with great powers comes great responsibility and we advise to only use it for production projects if you’re comfortable writing production quality code.
Unfortunately we don’t have the resources to support your custom code for obvious reasons, but our #developers community channel is very popular and a great place to ask questions.

Yes. You can simply copy and paste code components across projects and it will work. If you have a set of components that you would like to share with your team, you can organize them in a central project or even publish them as a mini website. If you write the component url to the clipboard, Framer can paste it and will load your component.

Framer components are React Components based on ES Modules. That means that you can technically import them into other projects, but in reality there are quite a few hurdles to overcome, so we only recommend this for testing or if you really know what you are doing. We had experimented with making the experience easier for this with a beta feature called Handshake. But as this relied on the Next.js compiler which is currently being rewritten and browser features that aren’t broadly supported yet, you should consider it very experimental for some time.

Importing npm packages is currently an experimental feature. Most packages typically don’t work unless they were built specifically for Framer. Some projects with multiple npm imports may run into errors with adding multiple npm dependencies, as sub-dependency conflicts can occur.

Framer can import any ES Module based code. But the code itself generally is only useful in Framer if it’s made for Framer. So importing large libraries that did not have Framer as the main use case in mind will likely not yield the expected results.

This may be alright in some cases, but if you need to do advanced logic, you are often better off with a real React application. Both Framer and your state management will try and control components, and conflicts can cause subtle bugs.
No. While many designers dream about a deeper design and production integration with code, Framer is not currently setup to get great results for that use case.

/developers/workspace-plugins.title: Framer Developers: Workspace Plugins
/developers/workspace-plugins.description: How to share Plugins with your Team
h3: Deploying a Plugin to a URL
p: Plugins are small apps that can be deployed on the web, just like a website. With Workspace Plugins you can deploy a Plugin once, add it via the Plugins modal on the dashboard, and instantly have it appear in the Plugin menu in every project in the Workspace. Once you have access to the feature, you will see a “Plugins” entry-point in the dashboard where you can go to manage the Plugins for your Workspace.
This feature is an add-on available for Enterprise teams at an additional cost. Contact your account manager for access or learn about Framer Enterprise.

From within the Plugins modal, you can add your Plugin URL. Workspace Plugins are self hosted, to give you full control to incorporate the Plugin into your internal systems and push updates instantly. When adding the URL, Framer will validate that it is set up correctly, and pull the name and icon info from your Plugin’s framer.json file.
To customise the Name and Icon of your Plugin, you'll want to customise the framer.json file. You can learn more about this on the configuration page.

Framer renders your Plugin URL directly in a secure iframe, so it will always point to the latest version each time the Plugin is opened. When updating the Modes, Icon, or Name of the Plugin, you will want to sync the updates into Framer by finding the Plugin in the Plugins modal on the dashboard, opening the context menu for that Plugin, and selecting ”Sync Info”.

Plugins are static assets and any Plugin created with npm create framer-plugin is setup for easy deployment. You can choose any static hosting you prefer, or can find instructions for using Vercel and Cloudflare below.
You will want to make sure the framer.json file is statically hosted at the root of your Plugin deployment. This will happen automatically if you use our default Plugin.

Framer uses the id field in your framer.json to differentiate each Plugin from one another, for example knowing which CMS Collection was synced by which Plugin. You’ll almost always want to ensure this value is unique, and Framer will warn when adding a Workspace Plugin with an ID that already exists in your Workspace. If you encounter this error, ensure you are uploading the correct Plugin and change the id if needed.
Read the getting started guide or follow these steps:
In the root of your Plugin directory run npx vercel
Follow the steps required to deploy to Vercel
Important: Log into your Vercel account and disable Vercel Authentication under Deployment Protection so that your deployment is publicly accessible
Now your plugin should be shareable in the URL displayed by Vercel.
Follow the steps in the getting started guide to setup your project
During configuration set npm run build for the build command
During configuration set ./dist for the build output directory
Now your plugin should be shareable in the URL displayed by Cloudflare.

/developers/comparison.title: Framer Developers: Comparison
/developers/comparison.description: When to use which Developer features
p: Framer offers a wide selection of features for Developers to use to extend the functionality of Framer. This page can help you decide how to choose between when to use Code Components, Overrides, Fetch, Plugins, or Custom Page Code.

Plugins are small apps that run within the Editor that can programmatically perform various tasks and utilize APIs to extend the core features of Framer. Plugins often utilize other features like Components to add functionality to the live website.

Fetch enables you to retrieve data from an API and use it on your Framer site without code. For Developers, this means you can set up endpoints for your team that work great with Fetch and allow your team to utilize the power of API calls from the client.

Components in Framer are core to adding interactivity and functionality to your live website. They can be created in Framer with or without Code. Code Components are React components that give you control to render anything within the Component.

Code Overrides are React Higher Order Components that can be applied to any Layer on your site. They are often used to override the properties of Layer or Components. Many previous uses for Overrides can now be achieved with Fetch or Components.

Custom Code in your site settings allows you to insert scripts and html at the start or end of the <head> and <body> tag of your site. Custom code and scripts can be added to specific pages or across every page on your published site.

/blog/radial-backgrounds/.title: Creating dynamic radial backgrounds with CSS and Framer Motion: UX Tutorial
/blog/radial-backgrounds/.description: Master advanced background techniques using CSS repeating-radial-gradients and Framer Motion. This technical guide shows UX designers how to implement dynamic, responsive background effects that enhance visual hierarchy and user experience.
h1: Advanced radial gradient techniques: dynamic backgrounds for professional UX
h3: Our favorite Framer website templates in September
Framer’s documentation toolkit: CMS, Search, Templates & more
p: Introducing a new component — the radial background component. This component combines CSS repeating-radial-gradient, background-position/size manipulation, and is powered by Framer Motion. In this blog post, we’ll dive into how it works.

The radial background component allows you to create endless radial patterns using two gradients, a few color stops, and varying background position/size combinations. This gives you greater control over the design of your project and enables you to create unique and dynamic backgrounds. See Radial Gradient.

With the radial background component, you can gain greater control over the size and position of your radial pattern. You can use background-size and background-position syntax separately rather than the repeating-radial-gradient() function shorthand syntax. This gives you more flexibility in designing your background and enables you to create more complex and intricate patterns.

The Framer component uses Framer Motion’s duration-based animations, providing the flexibility to specify a range of keyframes for orchestrating the pattern’s movement. This means you can create dynamic and interactive backgrounds that respond to user interactions or changes in the environment.

The radial background component is an exciting addition to Framer’s library that offers designers and developers greater control over the design of their projects. With its ability to create endless radial patterns, manipulate size and position, and use keyframe animations, this component opens up new possibilities for creating dynamic and interactive backgrounds.

/academy/lessons/fetch.description: Fetch enables you to leverage the power of APIs to add dynamic data to your Framer Site—without any code.
h1: Use Fetch to add dynamic data from APIs to your Framer Site
p: This lesson was released before Agents, Branching, and the CMS update on June 16, 2026. Some UI may differ, but the core concepts still apply.
Fetch enables you to leverage the power of APIs to add dynamic data to your Framer Site—without any code.

In this Framer tutorial, you will learn Use Fetch to add dynamic data from APIs to your Framer Site. We explain a practical workflow, highlight the key settings that affect the result, and show how to apply the technique on real pages for cleaner UX and better site performance. See How to use Fetch.
How do I set up a basic Fetch to pull external data into Framer?

For instance, you might set a navigation bar to fade in when the user scrolls past a section, and still maintain hover states on the links inside the bar. You do this by defining a scroll trigger (or scroll variant) for the section visibility, and then separately applying hover or click interactions to elements within the component. This layering allows for dynamic and engaging interactive behavior without losing the independent triggers.
What are typical use cases for Fetch in a Framer site?

Fetch is useful for displaying dynamic or real-time data that cannot be known at the time of publishing. Common examples include view counters, visitor location, live weather information, server status updates, and other API-based data such as stock prices, music playback, or sunrise and sunset times.
How do I handle loading states and error states when using Fetch?

When you add a Fetch to a component, Framer automatically creates special variants for Loading and Error states. Use the Loading variant to design what appears while data is being fetched, and the Error variant for when a request fails. You can customize both states completely, such as adding placeholder shapes or animations, and use opacity or effects to create smooth transitions when the fetched data appears.

/academy/lessons/framer-fundamentals-ana.title: Framer Academy: How to use Framer analytics to track visitors
/academy/lessons/framer-fundamentals-ana.description: Gain valuable insights into how your site and pages are performing.
h1: Tracking visitors with Framer’s built-in analytics
p: This lesson was released before Agents, Branching, and the CMS update on June 16, 2026. Some UI may differ, but the core concepts still apply.
Gain valuable insights into how your site and pages are performing.

In this Framer tutorial, you will learn Tracking visitors with Framer’s built-in analytics. We explain a practical workflow, highlight the key settings that affect the result, and show how to apply the technique on real pages for cleaner UX and better site performance. See Analytics Update.
How do I set up analytics tracking in Framer?

Analytics tracking is built into every Framer site automatically. After publishing your site, open the Analytics tab in the toolbar to view your data. Framer starts collecting and displaying metrics immediately, with no manual setup, tracking code, or external tools required.
What types of metrics can I track (pageviews, clicks, events) in Framer?

You can track a wide range of metrics in Framer’s built-in analytics: unique visitors, total pageviews, live-visitor counts (e.g., those active now), bounce rate, average session duration, traffic sources, UTM parameters, referring sites, top pages, countries, and device types. These insights appear automatically once you publish your site and can be filtered by date range. If you need more advanced tracking, such as detailed click events or custom conversions, you’ll likely want to integrate an external analytics tool or upgrade to a plan with those features.
How can I connect external analytics tools (e.g., Google Analytics) with Framer?

You can connect external analytics tools to your Framer site: for example, you can link Google Analytics by pasting your GA4 Measurement ID in the “Google Analytics” field under Site Settings, and Framer will handle the script automatically. If you’re using a different analytics provider, you can embed the tracking code yourself via the Custom Code section or a code component.

h2: General information about Framer’s Website and Service
